11Chain ruledy/dx = dy/du × du/dx, when y is a function of u, which is itself a function of x
⚡ SHORTCUT Product rule: "first times derivative of second, PLUS second times derivative of first." Quotient rule: same numerator pattern but with a MINUS, all over the denominator squared — mixing up the sign or which term gets differentiated first is the most common error with both.
FORMULA

Differentiation — Six Worked Examples (independently re-verified via symbolic computation) ★★★ HIGH

FunctionDerivative (verified)
y = x⁴By the power rule: 4x³
y = 1/xBy the negative power rule: −1/x²
y = x³+x²By the sum rule, applied term by term: 3x²+2x
y = x²·exBy the product rule: x²·ex + ex·2x = x²ex+2xex
y = 2x⁴By the power rule: 8x³
y = x⁴+4xBy the sum rule: 4x³+4

The quotient rule in full (independently re-verified)

Find dy/dx if y = x²/(x+1).

Let u=x² (so du/dx=2x) and v=(x+1) (so dv/dx=1). Applying the quotient rule: [v·du/dx − u·dv/dx] / v² = [(x+1)·2x − x²·1] / (x+1)².

Expanding the numerator: 2x²+2x−x² = x²+2x.

dy/dx = (x²+2x) / (x+1)².

CONCEPT

3.2 Revenue and Cost Function — Revenue ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Revenue refers to the receipts a firm obtains from selling quantities of a commodity at various prices. Three related concepts matter: Total, Average, and Marginal Revenue.

ConceptFormula and meaning
Total Revenue (TR)TR = P×Q, where P is price per unit and Q is quantity sold — the total money the firm receives.
Average Revenue (AR)AR = TR/Q = (P×Q)/Q = P. Average revenue is simply the price of the commodity itself.
Marginal Revenue (MR)The extra revenue earned from selling exactly ONE more unit: MR = TRn+1 − TRn. Equivalently, MR is the RATE OF CHANGE of total revenue with respect to quantity: MR = d(TR)/dQ, the slope of the total revenue curve.

Building an AR/MR schedule from TR data (independently re-verified)

Given the Total Revenue at each output level, find Average Revenue and Marginal Revenue at each point.

Q (units)TRAR = TR/QMR = TRn−TRn−1
00——
1292929
2542725
3722418
480208
580160
67212−8

Notice MR turns zero exactly where TR peaks (Q=5), and turns NEGATIVE once TR starts falling (Q=6) — a pattern worth recognising on sight.

CONCEPT

Cost, Profit, and the Break-Even Point ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Total Cost (TC) is everything a firm spends to produce a given output, split into two parts: TC = TFC + TVC.

  • Total Fixed Cost (TFC) does NOT change with output — rent, licence fees. Even at zero output, TFC is still paid.
  • Total Variable Cost (TVC) DOES change with output — raw materials, casual wages, transport. More output needs more of these.
ConceptFormula
Average Cost (AC)AC = TC / Output
Average Fixed Cost (AFC)AFC = TFC / Output
Average Variable Cost (AVC)AVC = TVC / Output
Marginal Cost (MC)MC = TCn+1−TCn, or as a derivative, MC = d(TC)/dQ — the extra cost of producing ONE more unit.
⚠ TRAP

Marginal cost ignores fixed cost entirely

THE TRAP: marginal cost is INDEPENDENT of fixed cost. Since fixed cost never changes with output, it contributes nothing to the CHANGE in cost from one more unit — there is no such thing as “marginal fixed cost.”

Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost. The Break-Even Point is where Profit = 0, i.e. where TR = TC exactly — the firm earns neither profit nor loss.

Profit maximises where MR = MC

Since Profit = TR−TC, setting d(Profit)/dQ = d(TR)/dQ − d(TC)/dQ = 0 gives MR−MC=0, i.e. MR=MC exactly — the single most important equilibrium condition in this whole topic, and the formal justification for why calculus is genuinely useful in business decision-making.

CONCEPT

3.3 Optimization Techniques — Slope and Curvature ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

For a differentiable function y=f(x), dy/dx (or f′(x)) is called the first derivative, and measures the SLOPE of the function at any point. Differentiating again gives the second derivative, f″(x) or d²y/dx², which measures how that slope is itself changing — the curve’s curvature.

A function is monotonically increasing if f′(x)>0 for every x in its domain (it rises continuously from left to right), and monotonically decreasing if f′(x)<0 throughout.

Recognising monotonicity directly from the derivative (independently re-verified)

f(x)=2x gives f′(x)=2>0, so this function is monotonically increasing.

f(x)=−6x gives f′(x)=−6<0, so this function is monotonically decreasing.

The SECOND derivative reveals curvature: if f″(x)>0, the curve is convex (curving upward, like a bowl); if f″(x)<0, the curve is concave (curving downward, like a dome).

f′(x)f″(x)Meaning
> 0> 0Rising at an increasing rate
> 0< 0Rising at a decreasing rate
< 0> 0Falling at an increasing rate
< 0< 0Falling at a decreasing rate
—= 0Changing at a perfectly constant rate, as with any straight line
FORMULA

Maxima and Minima — the First and Second Derivative Tests ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

At a curve’s peak (a Maximum) or trough (a Minimum), the tangent to the curve is perfectly horizontal, meaning the slope — the first derivative — is exactly zero at that point. This gives the necessary (first-order) condition for either a maximum or a minimum: f′(x)=0.

Since f′(x)=0 alone cannot distinguish a peak from a trough, a second test is needed: the sufficient (second-order) condition.

  1. If f″(x)<0 at that point, the curve is concave there, and the point is a relative Maximum.
  2. If f″(x)>0 at that point, the curve is convex there, and the point is a relative Minimum.
⚡ SHORTCUT Remember it as MAX-MINUS, MIN-PLUS: at a genuine Maximum, the second derivative is NEGATIVE; at a genuine Minimum, it's POSITIVE — the opposite of what many students instinctively guess.

A single-turning-point function (independently re-verified)

Find the value of x for which y=20x−2x² is optimum.

First-order condition: dy/dx=20−4x=0, giving x=5.

Second-order check: d²y/dx²=−4<0, so the function is maximum at x=5.

A function with TWO turning points requiring genuine discrimination (independently re-verified)

Find the maximum and minimum points of y=x³−9x²+15x+20.

First-order condition: dy/dx=3x²−18x+15=0, which factorises as 3(x−1)(x−5)=0, giving x=1 and x=5.

Second derivative: d²y/dx²=6x−18. At x=1, this gives −12<0. At x=5, this gives +12>0.

So y is maximum at x=1 and minimum at x=5 — the same first-order equation produced both a peak and a trough, and only the second derivative could tell them apart.

FORMULA

Applying Optimization to Business — Profit Maximisation ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

The same two-step test applies directly to a business Profit function, with the second-order condition confirming genuine profit MAXIMISATION rather than a minimum loss point.

Profit maximisation with a quadratic cost function (independently re-verified)

TR=20Q and TC=Q²+4Q+20. Find the profit-maximising output and the maximum profit.

Profit = TR−TC = 16Q−Q²−20. First-order condition: d(Profit)/dQ = 16−2Q = 0, giving Q=8.

Second-order check: d²(Profit)/dQ² = −2<0, confirming a genuine maximum at Q=8.

Maximum profit = 16(8)−8²−20 = 44.

Profit maximisation with a cubic cost function — two candidates to test (independently re-verified)

Price=₹4 per unit and TC=Q³−15Q²+31Q+100. Find the profit-maximising output and maximum profit.

TR=4Q, so Profit = 4Q−TC = −Q³+15Q²−27Q−100. First-order condition: d(Profit)/dQ = −3Q²+30Q−27=0, which simplifies to Q²−10Q+9=0, factorising as (Q−9)(Q−1)=0, giving Q=1 and Q=9.

Second derivative: d²(Profit)/dQ² = −6Q+30. At Q=1, this gives +24>0 (a minimum). At Q=9, this gives −24<0 (a genuine maximum).

So profit is maximised at Q=9, giving maximum profit = −27(9)−9³+15(9)²−100 = 143.

⚠ TRAP

A cubic cost function always gives you two candidates

THE TRAP: whenever the first-order condition is a QUADRATIC equation (as it is here, from a cubic Profit function), expect TWO solutions — and only the second-derivative test tells you which one is the genuine profit-maximising point and which is actually a local minimum (a loss-minimising trough). Never assume the larger, or the smaller, root is automatically the answer without checking.

MODULE 3 IN NINETY SECONDS — CALCULUS

① A function maps every x in its domain to exactly one (or more, if multi-valued) y. Nine types: constant, single/multi-valued, explicit/implicit, odd/even, inverse, polynomial, rational/irrational/algebraic.

② Limit: what f(x) approaches as x→a, even if f(x) isn't defined AT a. Three evaluation methods: factorisation, substitution, rationalisation.

③ Continuity at x=a needs left-limit = right-limit = f(a), all three equal.

④ Derivative = limh→0[f(x+h)−f(x)]/h. Eleven rules: power, negative power, eˣ, aˣ, ln, log_a, constant, sum/difference, product, quotient, chain.

⑤ TR=PQ, AR=P, MR=d(TR)/dQ. TC=TFC+TVC, MC=d(TC)/dQ (independent of fixed cost). Profit=TR−TC, maximised where MR=MC.

⑥ Optimization: f′(x)=0 is NECESSARY for both max and min. f″(x)<0 confirms MAX; f″(x)>0 confirms MIN — the sufficient condition.

⑦ A cubic Profit function gives a quadratic first-order condition — expect TWO critical points, and always run the second-derivative test on both.

MODULE FOUR OF EIGHT · SECTION B · 5% · STATISTICS BEGINS HERE

Statistical Representation of Data

Three sub-topics that turn raw data into a form you can actually read at a glance: diagrammatic representation using line, bar, and pie charts; frequency distribution as the tabular backbone of all descriptive statistics; and graphical representation of that same frequency data through histograms, frequency polygons, ogives, and pie-charts.

MUST NOT SKIP: the six types of bar diagram, the pie-chart angle formula (value/total × 360°), the discrete-vs-continuous frequency distribution distinction, and reading a cumulative frequency (ogive) curve.

4.1–4.3

Module Learning Objectives

Per ICMAI, after studying this Module the student will be able to understand: the meaning and definitions of Statistics; Statistical Methods; the representation of information through data; and different analysis of data.

Glossary — Terms Worth Knowing Cold

TermPlain meaning
FrequencyHow many times a particular value, or values within a class interval, occurs in the data.
Class intervalA range of values grouped together, e.g. 10–20, used when raw data has too many distinct values to list individually.
HistogramAdjacent bars over class intervals, with NO gaps between them (unlike a bar diagram).
OgiveA curve of CUMULATIVE frequency, either “less than” or “more than” type.
CONCEPT

4.1 Diagrammatic Representation of Data ★★ MEDIUM

Representing data through charts, diagrams, and pictures is attractive and accessible — unlike tabulation, it can be read by educated and uneducated audiences alike, and hidden trends often surface only when data is seen visually. Its trade-off is ACCURACY: diagrams are less precise than tabulated figures, so where precision matters most, tabulation remains the better choice. Three types are covered here: line diagrams, bar diagrams, and pie charts.

A Line Chart plots the independent variable (often time) along the horizontal axis and the dependent variable along the vertical axis; the plotted points are then joined to form a line, making trends over time easy to see at a glance.

A Bar Diagram represents data as a series of bars of uniform width, equally spaced, with each bar’s height (or length) proportional to the value it represents. Vertical bars suit cases where labels are written beneath each bar; horizontal bars suit cases where they are not, since the labels can then be read without turning the page. Convention favours bars WIDER than the gaps between them.

ICMAI recognises six types of bar diagram.

  1. Simple Bar Diagram: compares two or more items on a single variable; its limitation is that only ONE variable can be shown.
  2. Multiple, or Grouped, Bar Diagram: compares several items across two, three, or more values at once, using different shades or colours per category.
  3. Sub-divided, or Component, Bar Diagram: a single bar split into segments, where the whole bar is the aggregate and each segment is a component of it.
  4. Percentage Sub-divided Bar Diagram: the same idea as above, but every bar is rescaled so its segments total exactly 100%.
  5. Deviation, or Bilateral, Bar Diagram.
  6. Broken Bars.
CONCEPT

The Pie Chart — Construction and a Full Worked Example ★★★ HIGH

A Pie Chart (or Angular Diagram) is a circle whose total area represents the whole, divided into sectors whose sizes represent the component parts — named for the Greek letter π used in circle geometry. Since a full circle spans 360°, each component’s share of the total is converted into a proportional angle.

Angle for a component = (component value / total value) × 360°

Converting a frequency table into pie-chart angles (independently re-verified)

120 students chose work-experience options as follows: Photography 6, Clay Modelling 30, Kitchen Gardening 48, Doll Making 12, Book Binding 24.

AreaStudentsAngle
Photography6(6/120)×360 = 18°
Clay Modelling30(30/120)×360 = 90°
Kitchen Gardening48(48/120)×360 = 144°
Doll Making12(12/120)×360 = 36°
Book Binding24(24/120)×360 = 72°
Total120360°

All five angles sum to exactly 360°, confirming the calculation before drawing.

A second pie-chart example, for practice (independently re-verified)

A car dealer’s vehicle sales by type: Wagon R 72, S-Cross 54, Amaze 27, Punch 18, City 9. Total 180.

TypeNos. SoldAngle
Wagon R72(72/180)×360 = 144°
S-Cross54(54/180)×360 = 108°
Amaze27(27/180)×360 = 54°
Punch18(18/180)×360 = 36°
City9(9/180)×360 = 18°
Total180360°
CONCEPT

4.2 Frequency Distribution — Variables, Tally Marks, and Construction ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

A Variable (or variate) is any characteristic that differs from one individual to another — age, income, height, colour. QUANTITATIVE variables take numerical values (age, height); QUALITATIVE variables, also called attributes, take non-numerical values (colour, quality). Variables are further split into Continuous, which can take ANY value within an interval, including fractions (height, weight, temperature), and Discrete, which can take only whole, finite values (number of students in a class).

Tally Marks are a method of counting in blocks of five: a single stroke (|) represents 1, and the fifth stroke is drawn diagonally across the previous four, giving |||| for a count of 5. A Frequency Distribution is the ordered set {x,f}, showing every value x in the data together with its frequency f, or how many times it occurs. There are two types: Discrete Frequency Distribution, built directly by tallying each distinct value, and Grouped, or Continuous, Frequency Distribution, built by tallying values into class intervals instead of listing each one separately.

A frequency distribution table is constructed in five steps.

  1. Prepare three columns: the Variable (or class), Tally Marks, and Frequency.
  2. Arrange the data from lowest to highest in the first column.
  3. Take each observation in turn and mark a tally against it, recording tallies in bunches of five for easy counting.
  4. Count the tally marks for each row and record that count in the Frequency column.
  5. Give the table a suitable title that conveys exactly what it shows.
CONCEPT

Key Statistical Terms Worth Knowing Cold ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

TermMeaning
Raw DataStatistical data in its original form, before any technique has been applied to process or summarise it.
ArrayData arranged in order of magnitude — ASCENDING (lowest to highest) or DESCENDING (highest to lowest).
RangeThe difference between the largest and smallest values in the data.
Class / Class IntervalA group that the data has been divided into, bounded by class limits. The LOWER limit is the smaller boundary value, the UPPER limit the larger.
Class WidthUpper limit minus lower limit: I = U−L. Also called the range of a class.
Class Boundaries (true/actual class limits)Where a gap exists between adjacent classes, the limits are extended by half that gap to close it: Lower boundary = lower limit − ½ gap; Upper boundary = upper limit + ½ gap. In an EXCLUSIVE series, the class boundaries and class limits are identical.
Class Mark (mid-point, mid-value)The arithmetic mean of a class’s lower and upper limits: (Lower + Upper)/2.
Class MagnitudeUpper class BOUNDARY minus lower class BOUNDARY.

Ascending and descending arrays, and the range (independently re-verified)

Given the data 17, 7, 11, 5, 13, 9, form the ascending and descending arrays and find the range.

Ascending: 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17. Descending: 17, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5. Range = 17−5 = 12.

Building a grouped frequency table, then its class boundaries (independently re-verified)

Marks obtained by 18 students group into four classes: 1–10 (6 students), 11–20 (3), 21–30 (7), 31–40 (2).

This is an inclusive series (the gap between classes is 1 mark). The class boundaries of 11–20, for example, extend the limits by half that gap: Lower boundary = 11−0.5 = 10.5. Upper boundary = 20+0.5 = 20.5.

Class mark of 11–20 = (11+20)/2 = 15.5. Class magnitude of 20.5–30.5 = 30.5−20.5 = 10. Total students = 6+3+7+2 = 18.

A larger grouped table with class boundaries, from 100 raw daily-earnings figures (independently re-verified)

Daily earnings (₹) of 100 doctors, tallied into nine classes of equal width 10, give this frequency distribution.

Class (₹)FrequencyClass Boundaries
20–291319.5–29.5
30–391129.5–39.5
40–491839.5–49.5
50–591049.5–59.5
60–69659.5–69.5
70–79569.5–79.5
80–891479.5–89.5
90–991289.5–99.5
100–1091199.5–109.5
Total100—

This is an inclusive series (gap of 1 between class limits), so every boundary is the limit ±0.5, exactly as in the smaller example above.

CONCEPT

Inclusive vs. Exclusive Series, and Three Frequency Ratios ★★ MEDIUM

BasisInclusive SeriesExclusive Series
Also calledDiscontinuous seriesContinuous series
Upper limit treatmentINCLUDED in its own class, e.g. 0–5, 6–10, 11–15Becomes the LOWER limit of the next class, e.g. 10–15, 15–20, 20–25
Shared boundary pointNo overlap between classesThe shared value (e.g. 15 above) belongs to the HIGHER class
To make continuousMust be adjusted to class boundaries firstAlready continuous, no adjustment needed

Three further ratios describe a class’s frequency relative to the whole distribution.

  1. Relative Frequency = Class frequency ÷ Total frequency — the class frequency expressed as a fraction of the total.
  2. Percentage Frequency = (Class frequency ÷ Total frequency) × 100 — the same ratio expressed as a percentage.
  3. Frequency Density = Class frequency ÷ Class width — useful for comparing classes of UNEQUAL width fairly, since a wide class naturally accumulates more raw frequency without necessarily being more “dense.”
⚡ SHORTCUT Inclusive vs Exclusive, remembered by their names: INCLUSIVE includes the upper limit in ITS OWN class (0–5, 6–10 — no overlap). EXCLUSIVE excludes it from its own class by pushing it into the NEXT one (10–15, 15–20 — the boundary point "belongs up").
CONCEPT

4.3 Graphical Representation of Frequency Distribution ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Graphs of a frequency distribution present its characteristic features visually, making it easy to compare two or more distributions by shape and pattern. Four graphs are most commonly used: the Histogram, Frequency Polygon, Frequency Curve, and Cumulative Frequency Curve (or Ogive).

A Histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles, one per class, with NO gaps between them (unlike a bar diagram). The width of each class interval forms the base of its rectangle, and the height is proportional to that class’s frequency — when all classes are of EQUAL width, the class frequency itself can be used directly as the height.

Histogram with equal class widths (independently re-verified)

A distribution runs from 58–61 through 76–79 in seven equal-width classes, with frequencies 2, 10, 48, 64, 56, 16, 4.

Since every class has the same width, each rectangle’s height is simply set equal to its own class frequency, plotted against the class boundaries on the horizontal axis.

⚠ TRAP

Unequal class widths need Frequency Density, not raw frequency

THE TRAP: when class widths DIFFER, using raw frequency as the bar height would make wide classes look misleadingly “taller” just because they span more ground. The correct height is Frequency Density = Class Frequency ÷ Class Width, which keeps each rectangle’s AREA — not just its height — proportional to its frequency.

Histogram with unequal class widths, using frequency density (independently re-verified)

Class LimitsClass BoundariesWidthFrequencyDensity
10–149.5–14.5540.8
15–1914.5–19.55122.4
20–2919.5–29.510202.0
30–3929.5–39.510181.8
40–4939.5–49.510141.4
50–7449.5–74.525251.0
75–9974.5–99.525100.4

Plotting Frequency Density (not raw frequency) against the class boundaries gives a fair, undistorted histogram despite the varying widths.

CONCEPT

Frequency Polygon and the Ogive — One Complete Worked Example ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

A Frequency Polygon is drawn by joining the MID-POINTS of the tops of a histogram’s bars with straight lines, then closing the shape by extending it down to zero at one extra class-width on either side. An Ogive plots CUMULATIVE frequency against the class boundaries: a “less-than” ogive runs from 0 up to the total N, rising as each class is added in turn; a “more-than” ogive runs from N down to 0, falling as each class is subtracted away.

A complete wage-distribution example (independently re-verified)

Weekly wages of 65 employees fall into seven classes of equal width, 50–59 through 110–119, with frequencies 8, 10, 16, 14, 10, 5, 2.

For the FREQUENCY POLYGON, the mid-points of each bar’s top are joined in sequence, with the shape closed at zero on the class immediately before 50–59 and immediately after 110–119.

For the OGIVES, cumulative frequency is built up (less-than) and drawn down (more-than) at each class boundary:

Class Boundary“Less-than” c.f.“More-than” c.f.
49.5065 = N
59.5857
69.51847
79.53431
89.54817
99.5587
109.5632
119.565 = N0

The two ogive curves ALWAYS cross at exactly one point — and the value directly below that crossing point on the horizontal axis is the distribution’s Median, a graphical shortcut worth remembering.

⚡ SHORTCUT "Less-than" ogive: starts at 0, climbs to N — think of it as accumulating UP. "More-than" ogive: starts at N, falls to 0 — accumulating DOWN. Where the two curves cross, read straight down to the x-axis: that value is the Median.

MODULE 4 IN NINETY SECONDS — STATISTICAL REPRESENTATION

① Three diagram types: line (trend over time), bar (6 variants — simple/multiple/component/percentage/deviation/broken), pie (angle = value/total × 360°).

② Frequency distribution: {x,f} pairs, built via tally marks. Discrete (each value tallied) vs Grouped/Continuous (values tallied into class intervals).

③ Class boundary = limit ± half the inter-class gap. Class mark = (lower+upper)/2. Inclusive series (0–5, 6–10) vs Exclusive series (10–15, 15–20, boundary belongs to the higher class).

④ Relative frequency = class/total. Percentage frequency = that ×100. Frequency density = class frequency ÷ class width — use density whenever class widths are UNEQUAL.

⑤ Histogram: adjacent bars, no gaps, height = frequency (equal widths) or density (unequal). Frequency Polygon: join the bar-top midpoints, close at zero on both sides.

⑥ Ogive: cumulative frequency vs class boundary. "Less-than" rises 0→N; "more-than" falls N→0. Their crossing point's x-value is the Median.

MODULE FIVE OF EIGHT · SECTION B · 15% · A MAJOR MODULE

Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

Five sub-topics covering how to summarise a whole distribution in a single representative number, and how to measure how spread out it really is: Mean, Median, Mode, and Mean Deviation as measures of the CENTRE; Range, Quartiles, and Quartile Deviation; Standard Deviation, the single most important measure of spread; the Coefficient of Variation for comparing spread across different distributions; and Karl Pearson's and Bowley's measures of Skewness.

MUST NOT SKIP: all three methods of calculating the Arithmetic Mean, the Median formula for grouped data, Standard Deviation's direct and step-deviation methods, and the Coefficient of Variation formula for comparing two distributions.

5.1–5.5

Module Learning Objectives

Per ICMAI, after studying this Module the student will be able to understand: the concept of Averaging; the concept of Arithmetic Mean — different methods of computation with grouped and ungrouped data; the concept of Geometric Mean — different methods of computation with grouped and ungrouped data; the concept of Harmonic Mean — different methods of computation with grouped and ungrouped data; and the relation between Arithmetic Mean, Geometric Mean, and Harmonic Mean.

Glossary — Terms Worth Knowing Cold

TermPlain meaning
Central TendencyA single value that represents the whole distribution's centre — Mean, Median, or Mode.
DispersionHow spread out or scattered the data is around its centre.
Assumed Mean (A)A convenient reference value used to simplify calculation in the short-cut and step-deviation methods — the final answer does not depend on which value is chosen.
Weighted MeanA mean where each value's importance (its weight) differs, rather than every value counting equally.
CONCEPT

5.1 Measures of Central Tendency — the Arithmetic Mean ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Measures of central tendency split into two families: MATHEMATICAL measures (Arithmetic Mean, Geometric Mean, Harmonic Mean), calculated directly from every value, and POSITIONAL measures (Median, Mode), determined by a value’s position or frequency in the data rather than by calculation on every value.

The Arithmetic Mean (denoted X̄) can be calculated three ways for individual or discrete data.

MethodFormula
Direct MethodX̄ = ΣX / N
Short-Cut (Indirect) MethodX̄ = A + Σdx/N, where dx = X−A (deviation from an assumed mean A)
Step-Deviation MethodX̄ = A + (Σdx′/N)×i, where dx′=dx/i, and i is a common factor pulled out of every deviation

For GROUPED data (with frequency f), the same three methods apply with f folded in.

MethodFormula
Direct MethodX̄ = ΣfX / Σf
Short-Cut MethodX̄ = A + Σfdx/Σf
Step-Deviation MethodX̄ = A + (Σfdx′/Σf)×i

Combined Mean (2+ series): X̄ = (n₁X̄₁+n₂X̄₂+…+nkX̄k) / (n₁+n₂+…+nk)

Weighted Mean: X̄ = (w₁X₁+w₂X₂+…+wnXn) / (w₁+w₂+…+wn) — used whenever different values carry different importance, rather than counting equally.

Five Properties of the Arithmetic Mean are worth knowing:

  1. The sum of the deviations of the terms from the Actual Mean is always ZERO.
  2. The sum of the squared deviations of the items from the Arithmetic Mean is MINIMUM — less than the sum of squared deviations from any other value.
  3. Given the arithmetic mean and number of items of two or more groups, the COMBINED average of those groups can always be calculated.
  4. If the terms of a series are increased, decreased, multiplied, or divided by some constant, the mean is increased, decreased, multiplied, or divided by that SAME constant.
  5. The standard error of the arithmetic mean is LESS than that of any other measure of central tendency.
FORMULA

Arithmetic Mean — Five Worked Examples (independently re-verified) ★★★ HIGH

Direct method, individual data

Find the mean of 30, 41, 47, 54, 23, 34, 37, 51, 53, 47.

ΣX = 417, N = 10, so X̄ = 417/10 = 41.7.

Grouped data, discrete values

Marks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 were scored by 6, 12, 18, 15, 9 students respectively.

ΣfX = 24+96+216+240+180 = 756, Σf = 60, so X̄ = 756/60 = 12.6.

Grouped data with class intervals, using mid-points

Income classes 10–20 through 60–70 have frequencies 4, 7, 16, 20, 15, 8. Each class is represented by its mid-point (15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65).

ΣfX = 60+175+560+900+825+520 = 3,040, Σf = 70, so X̄ = 3040/70 = ₹43.43.

Correcting a mean after misread values

The mean of 20 terms was found to be 35, but two terms, 42 and 34, had been misread as 46 and 39.

Incorrect total = 35×20 = 700. Correct total = 700+42+34−46−39 = 691.

Correct mean = 691/20 = 34.55.

Finding one component's mean when the combined and other component's means are known

Factory A has 100 workers with a mean wage of ₹720/week; its 30 female workers have a mean wage of ₹650/week. Find the average wage of the male workers.

Total wage of all workers = 720×100 = 72,000. Total wage of female workers = 650×30 = 19,500. Total wage of male workers = 72,000−19,500 = 52,500. Male workers = 100−30 = 70.

Mean wage of male workers = 52,500/70 = ₹750 per week.

CONCEPT

Geometric Mean and Harmonic Mean ★★ MEDIUM

The Geometric Mean (g) is obtained by multiplying all n values together and taking the n-th root of the product: g = n√(X₁×X₂×…×Xn). In practice it is calculated via logarithms: g = Antilog[Σ(log X)/n] for individual data, or g = Antilog[Σf·log(X)/Σf] for grouped data (using mid-values for class intervals). Two properties are worth noting: the Geometric Mean is NEVER larger than the Arithmetic Mean, and can equal it only when all the values themselves are identical; and it is heavily used for averaging RATIOS, rates of growth, and index numbers.

Calculating the GM of a widely-spread income series (independently re-verified)

Find the GM of the monthly incomes: 180, 250, 490, 120, 1400, 7000, 1050, 150, 360, 100, 80, 200, 500, 240 (n=14).

Taking the sum of log₁₀ of all 14 values, dividing by 14, and taking the antilog gives g ≈ 340.56 — note how much closer this sits to the bulk of the data than a simple arithmetic mean would, since GM is far less distorted by the one extreme value (7,000).

The Harmonic Mean (H.M.) is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the values: H.M. = n / Σ(1/Xi) for ungrouped data, or H.M. = Σf / Σ(f/Xi) for grouped data. A Weighted H.M. = Σw / Σ(w/X). Harmonic Mean is the natural choice whenever averaging RATES defined per unit — speed (distance/time), price per unit, and similar quantities.

A weighted Harmonic Mean (independently re-verified)

Find the H.M. of 3, 6, 12, 24, whose respective weights are 6, 2, 4, 8.

Σw = 6+2+4+8 = 20. Σ(w/X) = 6/3+2/6+4/12+8/24 = 2+0.33+0.33+0.33 = 3.

H.M. = 20/3 = 6⅔.

⚡ SHORTCUT Choosing between the three means: AM for ordinary averaging of independent values. GM for averaging RATIOS, growth rates, and index numbers (anything multiplicative). HM for averaging RATES defined per unit, like speed or price-per-item (anything where you're really averaging 1/x).
CONCEPT

Median and Other Positional Measures ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

The Median (Md) is a POSITIONAL measure: the middle-most item once the data is arranged in order, dividing the series into two exactly equal halves.

CaseFormula
Individual series, n oddMd = value of the [(n+1)/2]th item, once arranged in order
Individual series, n evenMd = average of the (n/2)th and [(n/2)+1]th items
Discrete series with frequencyMd = value at the [(N+1)/2]th position, where N=Σf, read off the cumulative frequency column

Grouped data (“less-than” cumulative frequency): Md = l₁ + [(N/2−C)/f]×h

l₁ = lower boundary of the median class · N=Σf · C = cumulative frequency just BEFORE the median class · f = the median class’s own frequency · h = width of the median class.

Grouped data (“more-than” cumulative frequency): Md = l₂ − [(N/2−C″)/f]×h

l₂ = upper boundary of the median class · C″ = cumulative frequency just AFTER the median class. Both formulas, applied correctly to the same data, always agree.

FORMULA

Median — Four Worked Examples (independently re-verified) ★★★ HIGH

Individual series, odd count

Find the median of 17, 19, 21, 13, 16, 18, 24, 22, 20.

Arranged ascending: 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24. Here n=9, so Md is the (9+1)/2 = 5th item.

The 5th item is 19.

Individual series, even count

Find the median of 17, 19, 21, 13, 16, 18, 24, 22, 20, 26.

Arranged ascending: 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 26. Here n=10, so Md is the average of the 5th and 6th items: (19+20)/2.

19.5.

Discrete series with frequency

X = 10,20,30,40,50,60,70 with frequencies 4,7,21,34,25,12,3 (N=106).

The cumulative frequencies are 4, 11, 32, 66, 91, 103, 106. Md is the [(106+1)/2] = 53.5th item; since the c.f. jumps from 32 to 66 at X=40, every value from the 33rd through the 66th item is 40.

So the 53.5th item is 40.

Grouped data, verified BOTH ways

Classes 4–8 through 60–72 have frequencies 7, 12, 42, 56, 39, 22 (N=178). N/2=89, which falls in the class 28–40 (less-than c.f. reaches 61 before this class, 117 after) — the Median Class.

Using the less-than formula: l₁=28, C=61, f=56, h=12. Md = 28 + [(89−61)/56]×12 = 28 + 6 = 34.

Using the more-than formula instead (l₂=40, C″=61) gives the identical answer: Md = 34 either way.

CONCEPT

Mode — the Most Frequently Occurring Value ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

The Mode (M₀) is the value that occurs most frequently in a distribution. For individual or discrete series, simply identify whichever value repeats the most; if every value occurs exactly once, there is NO mode. A distribution can also be BI-MODAL (two values tied for most frequent) or multi-modal.

Grouped data: M₀ = l₁ + [(f₀−f₁) / (2f₀−f₁−f₂)] × h

l₁ = lower boundary of the modal class (the class with the HIGHEST frequency) · f₀ = frequency of the modal class itself · f₁ = frequency of the class just BEFORE it · f₂ = frequency of the class just AFTER it · h = width of the modal class.

Karl Pearson's empirical relationship: Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median)

Useful whenever one of the three measures is hard to calculate directly — such as with OPEN-ENDED classes, where no clear lower or upper boundary exists to anchor a direct Mean calculation.

FORMULA

Mode — Five Worked Examples (independently re-verified) ★★★ HIGH

Individual series

Find the mode of 12, 14, 16, 18, 26, 16, 20, 16, 11, 12, 16, 16, 20, 24.

16 appears 5 times, more than any other value, so Mode = 16.

Grouped data

Classes 0–10 through 60–70 have frequencies 4, 13, 21, 44, 33, 22, 7. The class 30–40 has the highest frequency (44), making it the modal class: f₀=44, f₁=21 (from 20–30), f₂=33 (from 40–50), l₁=30, h=10.

M₀ = 30 + [(44−21)/(2×44−21−33)]×10 = 30 + (23/34)×10 = 36.765.

Mode under a linear transformation

If y=12+1.5x and the mode of x is 15, find the mode of y.

Mode of y = 12+1.5×(mode of x) = 12+1.5×15 = 34.5 — the same linear transformation that relates x and y also relates their modes directly.

A memorable bi-modal example

Find the modal letter of the word “STATISTICS.”

S appears 3 times and T appears 3 times — more than any other letter, and tied with each other. The distribution is bi-modal: both S and T.

FORMULA

Open-Ended Classes — Finding the Mean via Median and Mode ★★★ HIGH

A full worked example tying Mean, Median, and Mode together (independently re-verified)

Price changes for 1,075 securities are classed from “below −10%” up to “10% and over,” both ends OPEN. Since the end classes have no defined boundary, the Arithmetic Mean cannot be calculated directly — only Median and Mode can, so the empirical relationship is used to find Mean.

Building the “less-than” cumulative frequency from the most negative class upward: 51, 82, 156, 256, 405, 751, 870, 941, 991, 1021, 1075. N/2 = 537.5, which falls in the class 0–2% (c.f. jumps from 405 to 751 there) — this is BOTH the median class (by position) AND the modal class (by having the highest single frequency, 346).

Median: l₁=0, C=405, f=346, h=2. Md = 0+[(537.5−405)/346]×2 = 0.7659.

Mode: f₀=346, f₁=149, f₂=119, l₁=0, h=2. M₀ = 0+[(346−149)/(2×346−149−119)]×2 = 0.9292.

Applying Mean−Mode=3(Mean−Median): Mean−0.9292 = 3(Mean−0.7659), which solves to Mean = 0.684 — found WITHOUT ever needing the undefined boundaries of the open-ended classes.

⚡ SHORTCUT Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median) rearranges to Mode = 3×Median − 2×Mean, or Mean = (3×Median − Mode)/2 — memorise whichever rearrangement matches what the question actually asks you to find.
CONCEPT

When to Use Which Average ★★ MEDIUM

AverageBest suited for
Arithmetic MeanGeneral-purpose averaging where every value counts equally.
Geometric MeanSeries with WIDE dispersion; constructing index numbers; averaging proportions, percentages, and compound rates; measuring population growth, which itself compounds geometrically.
Harmonic MeanProblems where SMALL items deserve more relative weight than large ones — time, speed, rates, and prices. Has limited use in practice otherwise.
MedianQualitative characteristics (honesty, intelligence, ability); distributions that are positively skewed; problems of income, wealth, and investment distribution.
ModeEveryday sizing problems — the modal collar size, modal shoe size, modal garment size — and applications across biology, meteorology, business, and industry.
CONCEPT

5.2 Dispersion — Why It Matters ★★★ HIGH

Dispersion is the degree of scatter, or variation, of individual values around a central value. Two distributions can share the exact SAME mean, yet look completely different once you see how tightly or loosely their individual values cluster around that shared centre — dispersion is what captures that difference.

Understanding dispersion matters for three reasons.

  1. It reveals how RELIABLE a measure of central tendency actually is — when individual items are widely spread, the mean, median, or mode is LESS representative of the distribution as a whole.
  2. Widely spread data carries its own peculiar problems, and dispersion helps locate them before they cause trouble.
  3. Comparing dispersion across samples helps identify highly fluctuating data, since more fluctuation generally means more risk.

When comparing two distributions with similar averages, the one with LESS dispersion (values clustering tightly around the centre) is generally the more reliable, more preferable option — a principle worth remembering when a question asks you to choose between two data sets or two shipment methods, forecasting models, and similar comparisons.

Measures of dispersion split into ALGEBRAIC measures (Range, Quartile Deviation, Mean Deviation, Standard Deviation, each with its own Coefficient for relative comparison) and GRAPHIC measures (the Lorenz Curve).

CONCEPT

Range and the Interquartile Range ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Dispersion is measured two ways: DISTANCE measures (Range, Quartile Deviation) and AVERAGE DEVIATION measures (Mean Deviation, Standard Deviation).

Range = Highest value − Lowest value   ·   Coefficient of Range = (Highest−Lowest) / (Highest+Lowest)

The Quasi Range excludes the two extreme values entirely: Quasi Range = 2nd-highest observation − 2nd-lowest observation.

Range, Quasi Range, and Coefficient of Range (independently re-verified)

Marks of 12 students: 52, 13, 35, 46, 89, 10, 29, 95, 66, 72, 48, 71.

Highest=95, lowest=10. Range = 95−10 = 85. Quasi Range = 89−13 = 76. Coefficient of Range = 85/105 = 0.810.

Range has four limitations worth knowing: it is easy to understand, but limited in usefulness; it uses ONLY the highest and lowest values, ignoring everything in between; being based on just two values, it can change drastically from one sample to the next; and it simply does not exist for an open-ended distribution.

FORMULA

Quartile Deviation — Splitting the Data Into Four ★★★ HIGH

Arranging data in order and splitting it into four EQUAL parts gives three cut points: Q₁ (first quartile, 25% of the way through), Q₂ (second quartile, the Median itself), and Q₃ (third quartile, 75% of the way through). The Interquartile Range = Q₃−Q₁ captures the spread of the MIDDLE half of the data.

CaseQ₁ formulaQ₃ formula
Individual/discrete series[(n+1)/4]th item, once arranged in order3×[(n+1)/4]th item
Grouped datal₁+[(N/4−C)/f]×hl₁+[(3N/4−C)/f]×h

For grouped data, l₁ = lower boundary of the respective quartile class · C = cumulative frequency just BEFORE that class · f = that class’s own frequency · h = its width — the same variables as the Median formula, just anchored at N/4 or 3N/4 instead of N/2.

Quartile Deviation (Semi-Interquartile Range) = (Q₃−Q₁)/2   ·   Coefficient of QD = (Q₃−Q₁)/(Q₃+Q₁)

Quartile Deviation from the same 12-student data (independently re-verified)

Sorted ascending: 10, 13, 29, 35, 46, 48, 52, 66, 71, 72, 89, 95. Splitting into 4 equal groups of 3: Q₁=29 (end of the first group), Q₃=71 (end of the third group).

Interquartile Range = 71−29 = 42. Quartile Deviation = 42/2 = 21.

A 20-item example (independently re-verified)

20 values sorted ascending give Q₁=70 (the 5th item) and Q₃=84 (the 15th item).

Interquartile Range = 84−70 = 14. Quartile Deviation = 14/2 = 7.

Quartile Deviation's merits: easy to calculate; works even with open-ended classes; and useful specifically for understanding variability in the central half of the data. Its demerits: it ignores fully 50% of the data (both tails); it doesn’t lend itself to further mathematical treatment; and technically, it doesn’t even measure genuine scatter around the average, since it’s based on position, not deviation.

⚡ SHORTCUT Both Range and Quartile Deviation use only 2 values from the whole dataset — Range uses the two extremes, QD uses Q₁ and Q₃. Neither is a true "average deviation" measure; both are purely positional/distance measures.
CONCEPT

Mean Deviation — the First True “Average Deviation” Measure ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Unlike Range or Quartile Deviation, Mean Deviation (or Average Absolute Deviation) genuinely uses EVERY observation. It is calculated in three steps: find the average (Mean, Median, or Mode — call it A); find the ABSOLUTE difference between each item and A, ignoring sign; and average those absolute differences.

Data typeFormula
Ungrouped dataM.D. = Σ|X−A| / n
Grouped dataM.D. = Σf|X−A| / Σf

Here A can be the Mean, Median, or Mode — Mean Deviation can be measured from any of the three.

Mean Deviation from the Mean, ungrouped data (independently re-verified)

Local conveyance payments to 12 officers: 863, 903, 957, 1041, 1138, 1204, 1354, 1624, 1698, 1745, 1802, 1883.

Mean = 16,212/12 = 1,351. Summing the absolute deviation of every value from 1,351 gives Σ|X−Mean| = 4,000.

M.D. = 4,000/12 = ₹333.3.

M.D.’s merits: easy to understand; based on ALL the items, not just extremes; and less affected by extreme values than Standard Deviation. Its demerits: using ABSOLUTE values ignores the sign of each deviation, a real weakness that motivates a more refined measure (Standard Deviation); and it doesn’t lend itself to further algebraic treatment.

FORMULA

Mean Deviation From Both Mean and Median, With Coefficients ★★★ HIGH

Coefficient of M.D. = Mean Deviation / (Mean or Median, whichever it was measured from)

Computing M.D. from BOTH Mean and Median in one pass (independently re-verified)

X = 3, 7, 12, 14, 15, 18, 22 (n=7). Mean = 91/7 = 13. Since n is odd, Median is the 4th sorted item = 14.

Summing |X−13| across all 7 values gives 34. Summing |X−14| gives 33.

M.D. from Mean = 34/7 = 4.86, Coefficient = 4.86/13 = 0.37. M.D. from Median = 33/7 = 4.71, Coefficient = 4.71/14 = 0.34.

⚡ SHORTCUT M.D. from Median is ALWAYS the smallest possible mean deviation you can get from any reference point — a genuine mathematical property, not a coincidence, worth remembering when a question asks which measure of central tendency minimises absolute deviation.

5.1 & START OF 5.2 IN NINETY SECONDS — AVERAGES AND FIRST DISPERSION MEASURES

① AM: 3 methods (direct/short-cut/step-deviation) for individual AND grouped data. Combined mean pools sub-group means; weighted mean weights unequal-importance values.

② GM (via logs) for ratios/growth/index-numbers; never exceeds AM. HM (reciprocal-based) for rates like speed/price-per-unit.

③ Median: (n+1)/2th item (odd) or average of two middle items (even), individual series; grouped data uses either the less-than OR more-than cumulative-frequency formula — both agree.

④ Mode: most frequent value; grouped formula uses f₀,f₁,f₂. Mean−Mode=3(Mean−Median) — solves for any one measure from the other two, vital for open-ended classes.

⑤ Dispersion = scatter around the centre; less dispersion means a MORE reliable central tendency. Range=Highest−Lowest. QD=(Q₃−Q₁)/2 — both are 2-value "distance" measures.

⑥ Mean Deviation = average of |X−A|, A=Mean/Median/Mode — the first TRUE average-deviation measure, using every value, though it discards the sign of each deviation.

CONCEPT

5.3 Standard Deviation — Variance and Its Square Root ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Variance (σ²) is the mean SQUARED deviation about the mean — squaring removes the sign problem that limited Mean Deviation, but leaves the units squared too (percent-squared, rupees-squared), which is hard to interpret directly. Standard Deviation (σ) fixes this by taking the square root of variance, returning to the ORIGINAL units.

MeasureDirect formulaShortcut (x²) formula
Variance (σ²)Σ(x−μ)² / NΣx²/N − μ²
Standard Deviation (σ)√[Σ(x−μ)²/N]√[Σx²/N − μ²]

Variance and S.D. from ungrouped data, both methods (independently re-verified)

15 impurity readings sum to 2.49, giving Mean = 2.49/15 = 0.166. Σ(x−m)² = 0.051, and separately, Σx² = 0.4643.

Direct method: Variance = 0.051/15 = 0.0034. Shortcut method: Variance = 0.4643/15 − (0.166)² = 0.0310−0.0276 = 0.0034 — both methods agree exactly.

Standard Deviation = √0.0034 = 0.058%.

The Empirical Rule: about 68% of values lie within ±1σ of the mean, about 95% within ±2σ, and about 99% within ±3σ

Standard Score (Z-score) = (x−m)/σ — tells you how many standard deviations a given observation sits above or below the mean. In the impurity example above, a reading of 0.108 gives Z=(0.108−0.166)/0.058=−1, meaning it sits exactly 1 S.D. below the mean.

FORMULA

Standard Deviation for Grouped Data — a Full Worked Example ★★★ HIGH

MeasureFormula
Variance (grouped)σ² = Σf(x−m)²/Σf = Σfx²/Σf − m²
Standard Deviation (grouped)σ = √[Σf(x−m)²/Σf]

Salary distribution across 12 classes, 100 people (independently re-verified)

Classes run from 700–799 through 1800–1899 (₹’000), with frequencies 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 17, 13, 10, 9, 7, 2, 1 (Σf=100). Using class mid-points, Σfx = 124,950.

Mean = 124,950/100 = 1,249.5. Working out f(x−m)² for every class and summing gives Σf(x−m)² = 6,680,000.

Variance = 6,680,000/100 = 66,800 (₹’000)². Standard Deviation = √66,800 = ₹258.46 (’000).

⚡ SHORTCUT Standard Deviation is the single most important dispersion measure precisely because it: (1) uses every observation, (2) never loses the sign problem that plagued Mean Deviation, since squaring makes everything positive automatically, and (3) supports the Empirical Rule for estimating what proportion of data falls in any given range — none of Range, QD, or MD can do that.
FORMULA

Standard Deviation — Shortcut and Step-Deviation Methods ★★★ HIGH

Beyond the direct method, two faster methods exist for calculating S.D. from grouped data.

MethodFormula
Shortcut Methodσ = √[Σfdx²/Σf − (Σfdx/Σf)²], where dx=x−A, A is an assumed mean
Step-Deviation Methodσ = √[Σfdx′²/Σf − (Σfdx′/Σf)²] × h, where dx′=(x−A)/h, h is a common factor (usually the class width)

Shortcut method (independently re-verified)

Ages of 480 people across 6 classes (20–25 through 45–50). Taking assumed mean A=32.5, working out fd and fd² for each class gives Σfd=−1,100 and Σfd²=32,750.

σ = √[32750/480 − (−1100/480)²] = √[68.23−5.25] = √62.98 = 7.936.

Step-deviation method, plus finding the Mean along the way (independently re-verified)

75 values across 7 classes (30–39 through 90–99). Taking A=64.5 and h=10, working out fd′ and fd′² for each class gives Σfd′=27 and Σfd′²=127.

Mean = 64.5+(27/75)×10 = 68.1. σ = √[127/75−(27/75)²]×10 = √[1.693−0.130]×10 = 12.505.

Standard Deviation of a Combined Series: σ₁₂ = √{[n₁(σ₁²+d₁²)+n₂(σ₂²+d₂²)] / (n₁+n₂)}

Where d₁=X̄₁₂−X̄₁, d₂=X̄₁₂−X̄₂, and X̄₁₂ is the combined mean = (n₁X̄₁+n₂X̄₂)/(n₁+n₂) — used whenever two groups’ individual means, S.D.s, and sizes are known, and the S.D. of the whole combined group is required WITHOUT re-processing every raw observation.

⚡ SHORTCUT Standard Deviation is NEVER computable from open-ended distributions, same limitation as the Mean — both need every class boundary defined. Step-deviation is the fastest of the three grouped-data methods whenever the class width h is constant across all classes.
CONCEPT

5.4 Coefficient of Variation ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

The Coefficient of Variation (C.V.) is the RELATIVE measure of dispersion based on Standard Deviation, expressed as a pure percentage with no units attached — which is exactly what makes it suitable for comparing the variability of two or more series, even when they’re measured in completely different units or scales.

C.V. = (Standard Deviation / Mean) × 100

A HIGHER C.V. means MORE variability in that data series. Since C.V. is unit-free, it is the correct tool whenever a question asks “which of these two is more variable/consistent/stable,” especially when the two series are on different scales.

Comparing variability across two differently-scaled series (independently re-verified)

Monthly electricity charges average ₹2,400 with S.D. ₹120. Monthly direct wages average ₹42,000 with S.D. ₹1,200. Which is more variable?

C.V. (electricity) = (120/2400)×100 = 5%. C.V. (direct wages) = (1200/42000)×100 = 2.9%.

Even though wages have a much LARGER absolute S.D. (₹1,200 vs ₹120), electricity charges are actually more variable RELATIVE to their own mean — exactly the kind of comparison C.V. is built for.

Solving for S.D. given the Mean and C.V. (independently re-verified)

A series has mean 10 and C.V. 40%. Find its S.D.

40 = (S.D./10)×100, so S.D. = 40×10/100.

S.D. = 4.

FORMULA

Five Properties of Standard Deviation, and How the Dispersion Measures Relate ★★ MEDIUM

  1. S.D. is independent of change of ORIGIN — adding (or subtracting) the same constant to every value leaves S.D. unchanged. The S.D. of 3, 4, 10, 19 equals the S.D. of 5, 6, 12, 21 (each term shifted by +2).
  2. S.D. is NOT independent of change of SCALE — multiplying every value by a constant scales the S.D. by that same constant. The S.D. of 4, 8, 14, 18 is exactly DOUBLE the S.D. of 2, 4, 7, 9.
  3. The sum of squared deviations taken from the Arithmetic Mean, Σ(X−X̄)², is always the MINIMUM possible such sum — smaller than if measured from any other reference point.
  4. The S.D. of the first n natural numbers = √[(n²−1)/12].
  5. For any set of observations, Standard Deviation is always ≥ Mean Deviation.

Relation between the dispersion measures: Q.D. = ⅔(S.D.)   ·   M.D. = ⅘(S.D.)

Also: Mean ± Q.D. covers roughly the middle 50% of the data; Mean ± M.D. covers roughly the middle 57.5%; and Mean ± S.D. covers roughly the middle 68% (matching the Empirical Rule).

⚡ SHORTCUT Remember the ratio chain QD : MD : SD = (2/3) : (4/5) : 1 — or equivalently 0.667 : 0.8 : 1 — a favourite fill-in-the-blank across all four papers whenever only one of the three is given and the other two must be derived.
CONCEPT

5.5 Skewness — When a Distribution Isn't Symmetrical ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Skewness is the asymmetry, or lack of symmetry, in a frequency distribution’s shape — specifically, how much further the curve extends on ONE side of its peak than the other. Skewness is best understood through how Mean, Median, and Mode relate to one another.

RelationshipCurve shape
Mean = Median = ModePerfectly SYMMETRICAL — zero skewness.
Mode < Median < MeanPOSITIVELY skewed — the tail stretches toward the RIGHT (higher values).
Mode > Median > MeanNEGATIVELY skewed — the tail stretches toward the LEFT (lower values).

In BOTH skewed cases, the Median always sits BETWEEN the Mode and the Mean, never outside them. A further characteristic, based on quartiles: for positive skew, Q₃−Md > Md−Q₁; for negative skew, Q₃−Md < Md−Q₁; for a symmetrical distribution, the two differences are exactly equal.

Three ABSOLUTE measures of skewness exist, each simply a difference between two central-tendency measures: SK = Mean−Mode, or SK = Mean−Median, or SK = Median−Mode. Being expressed in the original units, these can’t compare across differently-scaled distributions — which is exactly what the RELATIVE (coefficient) measures below are for.

FORMULA

Karl Pearson's and Bowley's Coefficients of Skewness ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Karl Pearson's Coefficient: Sk = (Mean−Mode) / S.D.

If Mode is hard to pin down or ill-defined, use the equivalent form instead: Sk = 3(Mean−Median) / S.D. Both versions range roughly ±3 in theory, though in practice values mostly fall within ±1. This is the coefficient USED MOST OFTEN in practice.

Bowley's Coefficient (Quartile measure of skewness): Sk = (Q₃+Q₁−2Md) / (Q₃−Q₁)

Ranges strictly between +1 and −1. Useful specifically when the mode is unclear, since it relies only on quartiles and the median, never on mode.

Kelly's Coefficient (percentile or decile skewness): Sk = (P₉₀+P₁₀−2P₅₀)/(P₉₀−P₁₀), or the decile equivalent using D₉, D₁, D₅. Ranges between ±1, but is seldom used in practice.

Karl Pearson's coefficient, directly from summary statistics (independently re-verified)

For 10 items, ΣX=452, ΣX²=24,270, and Mode=43.7.

Mean = 452/10 = 45.2. S.D. = √(24270/10−45.2²) = √383.96 = 19.595.

Sk = (45.2−43.7)/19.595 = 0.08 — a mild positive skew.

FORMULA

CV and Skewness Together — Two Distributions Compared ★★★ HIGH

A genuinely important exam pattern: two distributions can be claimed to have “the same variability and skewness” — checking BOTH claims independently often reveals one is true and the other false, or that neither holds.

Where variability differs but skewness happens to match (independently re-verified)

Distribution A: Mean=100, Median=90, S.D.=10. Distribution B: Mean=90, Median=80, S.D.=10. Claimed: (i) same variability, (ii) same skewness.

C.V.(A) = 10/100×100 = 10%. C.V.(B) = 10/90×100 = 11.11%. Since these differ, claim (i) is FALSE.

Sk(A) = 3(100−90)/10 = 3. Sk(B) = 3(90−80)/10 = 3. These are IDENTICAL, so claim (ii) is TRUE — variability and skewness can genuinely diverge in their conclusions about the very same pair of distributions.

Where skewness is not just different, but opposite in DIRECTION (independently re-verified)

Factory A: Mean=₹50, Mode=₹45, Variance=100. Factory B: Mean=₹45, Mode=₹50, Variance=100. Claimed: skewness and variability are the same in both.

S.D. = √100 = 10 for both. C.V.(A) = 10/50×100 = 20%. C.V.(B) = 10/45×100 = 22.22% — variability claim is FALSE.

Sk(A) = (50−45)/10 = +0.5 (positive skew). Sk(B) = (45−50)/10 = −0.5 (negative skew) — not merely different in size, but OPPOSITE in direction, making the skewness claim doubly false.

⚡ SHORTCUT Always check the SIGN of Karl Pearson's Sk before its magnitude — swapping which value is Mean and which is Mode (or Median) flips the sign entirely, turning a positive skew claim into a negative one, exactly as Factory A vs B demonstrates.

MODULE 5 IN NINETY SECONDS — CENTRAL TENDENCY & DISPERSION, COMPLETE

① Central tendency: AM (3 methods), GM (ratios/growth), HM (rates), Median (positional, odd/even/grouped), Mode (most frequent; Mean−Mode=3(Mean−Median)).

② Dispersion, distance measures: Range=Highest−Lowest. QD=(Q₃−Q₁)/2 — both use only 2 values.

③ Dispersion, average-deviation measures: MD=Σ|X−A|/n (A=Mean/Median/Mode). SD=√[Σ(X−Mean)²/N], the most important measure — 3 grouped methods (direct/shortcut/step-deviation).

④ QD:MD:SD = ⅔:⅘:1. CV=SD/Mean×100 — the ONLY unit-free measure, essential for comparing differently-scaled distributions.

⑤ Skewness: Mean=Median=Mode → symmetrical. Mode<Median<Mean → positive skew (tail right). Mode>Median>Mean → negative skew (tail left).

⑥ Karl Pearson's Sk=(Mean−Mode)/SD, most-used in practice. Bowley's Sk=(Q₃+Q₁−2Md)/(Q₃−Q₁), ranges ±1. CV and Skewness can diverge — always check BOTH independently, never assume one implies the other.

MODULE SIX OF EIGHT · SECTION B · 15% · A MAJOR MODULE

Correlation and Regression

Three sub-topics covering how two variables relate to each other: the Scatter Diagram as a first visual read on whether a relationship exists; Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation for measuring the STRENGTH and direction of a linear relationship precisely; and Regression Analysis for actually predicting one variable from the other.

MUST NOT SKIP: the −1 to +1 interpretation scale for the correlation coefficient, Karl Pearson's formula itself, the distinction between correlation (association) and regression (prediction), and the two regression line equations.

6.1–6.3

Module Learning Objectives

Per ICMAI, after studying this Module the student will be able to: understand the concept and types of correlation; construct and interpret a scatter diagram; calculate and interpret Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation; and apply simple linear regression to predict one variable from another.

Glossary — Terms Worth Knowing Cold

TermPlain meaning
CorrelationThe degree to which two variables are LINEARLY associated with each other — it does not, by itself, imply that one causes the other.
RegressionA technique for predicting the value of one variable from the value of another, using a fitted straight line.
Scatter DiagramA plot of paired (X,Y) points, used to visually judge whether and how two variables relate.
CONCEPT

6.1 Correlation Analysis — Meaning and Types ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Correlation is the statistical tool that measures the degree to which one variable is LINEARLY related to another — useful ONLY for linear relationships; it offers no help for other kinds of association between variables.

Correlation classifies along three separate dimensions.

  1. Positive (direct) vs. Negative (inverse): POSITIVE means the two variables move in the SAME direction — both rise together or both fall together. NEGATIVE means they move in OPPOSITE directions — one rises as the other falls.
  2. Simple vs. Multiple: SIMPLE correlation studies the relationship between exactly two variables, such as height and weight, or price and demand. MULTIPLE correlation studies one variable’s relationship with two or more OTHER variables taken together.
  3. Partial vs. Total: PARTIAL correlation studies the relationship between two variables while holding one or more OTHER variables constant — for instance, rainfall’s relationship with crop yield, ignoring the separate effects of fertiliser or seed quality. TOTAL correlation studies all the variables together at once.
FORMULA

Interpreting the Correlation Coefficient (r) ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Karl Pearson’s Coefficient of Correlation, r, always falls between −1 and +1 inclusive: −1≤r≤1. r=+1 means PERFECT positive correlation; r=−1 means PERFECT negative correlation; r=0 means NO correlation at all.

Value of rInterpretation
r = +1Perfect positive correlation
0.75 < r < 1High degree of positive correlation
0.5 < r < 0.75Moderate degree of positive correlation
0 < r < 0.5Low degree of positive correlation
r = 0No correlation at all
−0.5 < r < 0Low degree of negative correlation
−0.75 < r < −0.5Moderate degree of negative correlation
−1 < r < −0.75High degree of negative correlation
r = −1Perfect negative correlation
⚠ TRAP

A book misprint, corrected here

THE TRAP: the source prints the “high negative correlation” row as “1 < r < −0.75,” which is a logically impossible range (1 is never less than −0.75). Mirroring the positive side’s own structure, this is corrected to −1 < r < −0.75 above — use the corrected version.

CONCEPT

Scatter Diagram — Reading the Pattern of Dots ★★ MEDIUM

A Scatter Diagram plots one dot for every (X,Y) pair in the data. The overall SHAPE the dots form gives a quick, visual first read on whether — and how strongly — two variables are correlated, well before any formula is applied.

Pattern of dotsInterpretation
A single straight line, rising left-to-rightPerfect positive correlation (r=+1)
A single straight line, falling left-to-rightPerfect negative correlation (r=−1)
A loosely rising cloud of pointsLow-to-moderate positive correlation
A loosely falling cloud of pointsLow-to-moderate negative correlation
A shapeless, directionless cloudNo correlation (r≈0)

Scatter Diagram’s advantages: genuinely easy to draw; easily understood and interpreted even by a non-specialist audience; and extreme items don’t unduly distort the overall picture, since they simply remain isolated points rather than pulling a calculation off course. Its disadvantages: it gives no PRECISE numerical degree of correlation; and it doesn’t lend itself to further mathematical treatment.

FORMULA

6.2 Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Scatter diagrams and graphic methods are too subjective for precise work — in practice, linear correlation is measured through Karl Pearson’s Method (also called the Covariance Method).

r = Σ[(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ)] / √[Σ(X−X̄)² × Σ(Y−Ȳ)²]

Equivalently, r = Cov(x,y) / (σx·σy), where Cov(x,y) = Σ[(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ)]/N is the Covariance between X and Y, and σx, σy are the two series’ own Standard Deviations.

Correlation between father's and son's height (independently re-verified)

Fathers’ heights: 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70. Sons’ heights: 66, 67, 65, 68, 70, 68, 72 (n=7).

Mean of X = 469/7 = 67. Mean of Y = 476/7 = 68. Working out (X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ), (X−X̄)², and (Y−Ȳ)² for every pair and summing gives Σ(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ)=25, Σ(X−X̄)²=28, Σ(Y−Ȳ)²=34.

r = 25/√(28×34) = 25/30.85 = 0.81 — a high degree of positive correlation between fathers’ and sons’ heights.

Computational shortcut (avoids computing every deviation from the mean by hand): r = [NΣXY−(ΣX)(ΣY)] / √{[NΣX²−(ΣX)²][NΣY²−(ΣY)²]}

Indirect (assumed-mean) method: r = [NΣdx·dy−(Σdx)(Σdy)] / √{[NΣdx²−(Σdx)²][NΣdy²−(Σdy)²]}

Where dx=X−A, dy=Y−B, with A and B as assumed means for the X and Y series respectively — useful when the actual means turn out to be inconvenient, non-round numbers.

⚡ SHORTCUT All these formulas compute the exact SAME r — they're just different arithmetic routes to it. Pick whichever is fastest for the numbers in front of you: direct deviations when the means are already round numbers, the computational shortcut when they aren't, and the assumed-mean method for grouped or awkward data.
CONCEPT

Properties of Karl Pearson's Coefficient ★★ MEDIUM

  1. r always lies between ±1; if no correlation exists, r=0.
  2. It is based on ALL items of the variable, making it a genuinely comprehensive measure.
  3. It measures both the DIRECTION and the DEGREE of change together.
  4. An accidental (“non-sense” or spurious) correlation can produce a misleadingly high r with no real relationship behind it.
  5. Correlation does NOT prove causation — it only measures co-variation. Two variables can move together due to a common cause, mutual dependence, chance, or genuine causation, and r alone cannot distinguish between these.
  6. It is independent of change of scale and origin.
  7. r is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients: r = ±√(byx·bxy).
  8. It is independent of the unit of measurement.
  9. It works both ways: rxy = ryx.
  10. If y=ax+b (a positive), r is positive; if y=−ax+b (a positive), r is negative.
FORMULA

Probable Error — Is r Actually Significant? ★★★ HIGH

Probable Error (P.E.) measures the reliability of a correlation coefficient calculated from a SAMPLE, since sampling naturally introduces error.

P.E. = 0.6745 × (1−r²)/√N

Interpreting r against its P.E. follows clear rules: if r < P.E., there is NO evidence of correlation. If r > P.E. but r ≤ 6×P.E., correlation exists but is NOT significant. If r > 6×P.E., the correlation IS significant. The limits r±P.E. give the range within which correlation coefficients from other random samples of the same population would likely fall.

Testing significance (independently re-verified)

r=0.69 between advertising expenditure and sales, from 9 items. Test its significance.

P.E. = 0.6745×(1−0.69²)/√9 = 0.6745×0.5239/3 = 0.118. 6×P.E. = 0.708.

Since r=0.69 < 0.708, r is NOT significant despite being a fairly large number on its own.

Finding confidence limits (independently re-verified)

A sample of 100 gives r=0.9 between weight and height. Find the limits within which this holds for the whole population.

P.E. = 0.6745×(1−0.9²)/√100 = 0.6745×0.19/10 = 0.0128.

Limits = 0.9±0.0128, i.e. 0.887 to 0.913.

FORMULA

Rank Correlation (Spearman's Method) ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Devised by Charles Spearman in 1904, Rank Correlation is based on the RANKS of items rather than their actual values — ideal when raw values aren’t available, only rankings, or when comparing an abstract quality (like beauty, or honesty) that can only be ranked, not measured directly.

rk = 1 − [6ΣD² / N(N²−1)]

D = the difference between a pair’s two ranks, N = number of pairs. Like Pearson’s r, rk also always falls between −1 and +1.

Case I — ranking raw values directly (independently re-verified)

Six paired (X,Y) observations. Ranking each series separately and finding D=R₁−R₂ for every pair gives ΣD²=20.

rk = 1−[6×20 / 6×(36−1)] = 1−(120/210) = 1−0.571 = 0.429.

Case III — Tied ranks: when two or more items tie, each gets the AVERAGE of the ranks they’d otherwise occupy — e.g. two items tied for 3rd place both get (3+4)/2=3.5. The formula then needs a correction term added for every group of tied items.

rk = 1 − {6[ΣD² + Σ(1/12)(m³−m)]} / (N³−N)

Where each m is the size of one group of tied ranks, and (1/12)(m³−m) is added ONCE for every such group.

Case III — with tied ranks (independently re-verified)

8 students’ marks in Accountancy and Economics. Accountancy has a tie of 2 students (both ranked 5.5); Economics has a tie of 3 students (all ranked 5). Working out D² for every pair gives ΣD²=81.5.

Correction = (1/12)(2³−2) + (1/12)(3³−3) = (1/12)(6)+(1/12)(24) = 0.5+2 = 2.5. Adjusted ΣD² = 81.5+2.5 = 84.

rk = 1−(6×84)/(8³−8) = 1−(504/504) = 0 — a genuinely surprising result given several individual differences looked substantial, showing why the full calculation matters more than eyeballing the data.

⚡ SHORTCUT Spot which formula a question wants fast: raw VALUES given → Karl Pearson's r. Only RANKS or ORDERING given (or an abstract quality like skill/beauty) → Spearman's r_k. Any tie in either ranking → don't forget the correction term.
FORMULA

Concurrent Deviation Method ★★ MEDIUM

The Concurrent Deviation Method is a quick, rough method of correlation that looks ONLY at the DIRECTION of change in each variable from its own preceding value — not the magnitude — marking every step ‘+’ for an increase and ‘−’ for a decrease.

r = ±√[±(2C−N)/N]

C = number of CONCURRENT deviations (steps where the two series’ signs match), N = number of pairs of deviations compared (one less than the number of original observations, since the first item has no preceding value to compare against).

⚠ TRAP

Getting the sign right

THE RULE: if (2C−N)/N comes out NEGATIVE, you can’t take a square root of a negative number — so multiply it by −1 to make the value under the root positive, take that square root, and then put a MINUS sign in front of the whole result. If (2C−N)/N is already positive, both the inside and outside signs stay positive.

Steel output vs. unemployment, 12 months (independently re-verified)

Monthly output of steel and monthly unemployed workers in the steel industry, January–December. Marking ‘+’ or ‘−’ for each month’s change from the PREVIOUS month (11 comparisons possible from 12 months) and comparing the two sign-sequences gives 2 months where the signs concur (matching directions) and 9 where they don’t — so C=2, N=11.

r = ±√[±(2×2−11)/11] = ±√[±(−7/11)] = −√(7/11) = −√0.636 = −0.798 — a fairly high degree of NEGATIVE correlation between steel output and steel-industry unemployment, computed without ever using the actual output or unemployment figures, only their month-to-month direction of change.

⚡ SHORTCUT Concurrent Deviation is the FASTEST of the three correlation methods — no ranking, no squaring, no summing of products — but also the ROUGHEST, since it throws away everything except direction of change. Use it only for a quick approximate read, never as a substitute for Karl Pearson's r when precision matters.
CONCEPT

6.3 Regression Analysis — Predicting One Variable From Another ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Regression Analysis is the statistical technique for estimating or predicting the unknown value of a DEPENDENT variable from the known value of an INDEPENDENT variable. Sir Francis Galton introduced the concept in 1877, studying the relationship between fathers’ and sons’ heights.

Regression serves four objectives: explaining variation in the dependent variable through the independent variable(s); describing the relationship precisely via a regression EQUATION; supporting prediction and forecasting; and helping remove the effect of unwanted, confounding factors.

Regression classifies two ways.

BasisTypes
Number of variablesSimple (one dependent, one independent) · Partial (more variables exist, but only two are analysed at a time, others held constant) · Multiple (one dependent variable, more than one independent variable)
Change in proportionLinear (a straight-line relationship) · Non-linear (a curved relationship)

There are two distinct regression equations, since prediction can run in either direction.

  • Regression equation of Y on X (form: Y=a+bX), used when Y is dependent and X is independent.
  • Regression equation of X on Y (form: X=a+bY), used when X is dependent and Y is independent.
FORMULA

Finding the Regression Line — Two Methods ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Method 1, Normal Equations: ΣY=Na+bΣX   and   ΣXY=aΣX+bΣX²

Solving these two equations simultaneously gives a and b directly for Y=a+bX. For X=a+bY, the parallel normal equations are ΣX=Na+bΣY and ΣXY=aΣY+bΣY².

Method 2, Regression Coefficients: byx = Σ(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ) / Σ(X−X̄)²   ·   bxy = Σ(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ) / Σ(Y−Ȳ)²

Once byx is known, the line Y on X is: Y−Ȳ = byx(X−X̄). Once bxy is known, the line X on Y is: X−X̄ = bxy(Y−Ȳ).

Finding BOTH regression equations (independently re-verified)

10 paired observations of Sales (X) and Purchase (Y). X̄=900/10=90, Ȳ=700/10=70. Working out (X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ), (X−X̄)², and (Y−Ȳ)² for every pair and summing gives Σ(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ)=3,900, Σ(X−X̄)²=6,360, Σ(Y−Ȳ)²=2,868.

byx = 3900/6360 = 0.613. bxy = 3900/2868 = 1.36.

Regression of Y on X: Y−70=0.613(X−90), giving Y = 0.613X + 14.83. Regression of X on Y: X−90=1.36(Y−70), giving X = 1.36Y − 5.2.

Key relationship: r² = byx × bxy, so r = ±√(byx×bxy)

The correlation coefficient is the GEOMETRIC MEAN of the two regression coefficients — a genuinely useful cross-check: if you’ve calculated both byx and bxy, you can verify r without recomputing it from scratch. Also: bxy = r·(σx/σy) and byx = r·(σy/σx).

⚡ SHORTCUT Correlation is symmetric (r_xy = r_yx, one single number), but Regression is NOT — there are always two distinct lines (Y on X, and X on Y), and mixing up which coefficient (b_yx vs b_xy) belongs to which line is the single most common error in this topic.
CONCEPT

Properties of Regression Coefficients ★★ MEDIUM

  1. The two regression coefficients cannot BOTH exceed unity at the same time — since byx·bxy=r²≤1, if one coefficient is greater than 1, the other must be less than 1 to compensate.
  2. Both regression coefficients always carry the SAME sign: if bxy is positive, byx is also positive (and r is positive); if bxy is negative, byx is also negative (and r is negative).
  3. The correlation coefficient is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients: r = ±√(bxy·byx).
  4. The ARITHMETIC MEAN of the two regression coefficients is always ≥ the correlation coefficient: (bxy+byx)/2 ≥ r.
  5. Regression coefficients are independent of change of ORIGIN but NOT of scale.

Cross-checking r from the two regression coefficients (independently re-verified)

Household income and expenditure data gives: average absolute increase in income per unit increase in expenditure, bxy=1.5; average absolute increase in expenditure per unit increase in income, byx=0.5.

r = ±√(1.5×0.5) = √0.75 = 0.866 — positive, since both regression coefficients are positive. Note that bxy=1.5 exceeds unity here, which is fine since byx=0.5 is below it — only their PRODUCT is constrained to ≤1.

CONCEPT

Correlation vs. Regression — How They Relate and Differ ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Relation: the two regression lines COINCIDE into a single line when correlation is perfect (r=±1). When r=0 (the variables are independent), the two lines cut each other at right angles, running parallel to the axes. The closer |r| is to 1, the CLOSER the two regression lines sit to each other; the lower |r| is, the WIDER the gap between them. Wherever the two lines intersect, that point always gives the means (X̄, Ȳ) of the two series.

BasisCorrelationRegression
NatureTests the CLOSENESS between the variables.Measures the EXTENT of change in the dependent variable due to change in the independent variable.
DependenceStudies the MUTUAL dependence of variables; both are treated at par, for study purposes.Studies the FUNCTIONAL relationship, with one variable depending on the other; variables are differentiated as dependent and independent.
Spurious resultsCan suffer from spurious (“non-sense”) correlation with no practical importance.No such possibility of a spurious relationship.
Further treatmentHas no scope for further mathematical treatment.Can be used for further statistical treatment.
Origin & scaleIndependent of change of BOTH origin and scale.Independent of change of origin, but NOT of scale.
Type of measureA RELATIVE measure of linear relationship, confined between −1 and +1.An ABSOLUTE measure, showing the actual change in the value of Y (or X) for a unit change in X (or Y).
ScopeLimited — only linear relationships between two variables.Much wider — covers both linear and non-linear relationships.
SymmetrySYMMETRICAL in formation: rxy = ryx.ASYMMETRICAL in formation: bxy ≠ byx in general.
FORMULA

Standard Error of Estimate ★★ MEDIUM

The Standard Error of Estimate (Se) measures the reliability of a fitted regression equation — the degree to which actual Y values scatter around the values (Yc) computed from the regression line.

Se = √{[ΣY² − aΣY − bΣXY] / (n−2)}

The LARGER Se is, the greater the scatter of points around the regression line; if Se=0, every actual Y value lies exactly on the regression line for the given X values. Assuming the points are normally distributed around the regression line: 68% of the points lie within ±1 Se, 95.5% lie within ±2 Se, and 99.7% lie within ±3 Se.

MODULE 6 IN NINETY SECONDS — CORRELATION & REGRESSION, COMPLETE

① Correlation measures LINEAR association only; doesn't prove causation. Types: positive/negative, simple/multiple, partial/total.

② r ranges −1 to +1. Scatter Diagram gives a quick visual read; Karl Pearson's r = Σ(X−X̄)(Y−Ȳ)/√[Σ(X−X̄)²×Σ(Y−Ȳ)²] gives the precise value.

③ Probable Error = 0.6745×(1−r²)/√N tests significance — r must exceed 6×P.E. to be significant.

④ Rank Correlation (Spearman): rk=1−6ΣD²/N(N²−1), for ranked/abstract data — add the (1/12)(m³−m) correction for every group of tied ranks.

⑤ Concurrent Deviation: r=±√[±(2C−N)/N], a quick rough method using only the DIRECTION of change (C=concurrent deviations, N=pairs of deviations compared).

⑥ Regression predicts one variable from another — TWO distinct lines exist (Y on X, X on Y), found via normal equations OR regression coefficients (byx, bxy).

⑦ r²=byx×bxy links correlation and regression together — a useful cross-check between the two topics.

MODULE SEVEN OF EIGHT · SECTION B · 15% · A MAJOR MODULE

Probability

Two sub-topics building the language and toolkit of probability: Concepts and Terminologies covering the essential vocabulary (sample space, events, mutually exclusive, independent) and the classical approach to measuring probability; and the primary application theorems — Addition and Multiplication — for combining probabilities across multiple events.

MUST NOT SKIP: the exact definitions of mutually exclusive, exhaustive, and independent events (they are frequently confused with each other), the classical probability formula, and the Addition and Multiplication theorems with their conditional forms.

7.1–7.2

Module Learning Objectives

Per ICMAI, after studying this Module the student will be able to understand: the principal concepts and features of Probability; the application of Permutation and Combination in solving problems of Probability; Sample Space and the various theories of Probability; Conditional Probability and the Rule of Total Probability; Bayes’ Theorem; and the application of probability in the real world.

Glossary — Terms Worth Knowing Cold

TermPlain meaning
Random ExperimentA repeatable action whose individual outcome cannot be predicted in advance, though all POSSIBLE outcomes are known.
Sample SpaceThe complete set of every possible outcome of a random experiment.
EventAny outcome, or set of outcomes, of a random experiment.
Mutually ExclusiveEvents that CANNOT occur together — one happening rules out the other in that same trial.
Independent EventsEvents where one occurring does NOT affect the probability of the other.
CONCEPT

7.1 Probability — the General Concept ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Probability denotes the likelihood of an event occurring, expressed as a number between 0 and 1. A probability of 0 means the event is IMPOSSIBLE; a probability of 1 means the event is CERTAIN. Everything in between represents a genuine fraction of a chance — for a fair coin toss, the probability of heads is exactly ½, since heads and tails share the chance equally.

CONCEPT

Eleven Terms That Are Frequently Confused ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

TermMeaning
Random Experiment / TrialAn action repeatable under the same conditions, where the total set of possible outcomes is known but the individual outcome of any one repetition is NOT predictable — e.g. tossing a coin.
OutcomeA possible result of a random experiment — tossing a coin has outcomes H and T.
EventAny possible outcome of a random experiment. A SIMPLE event corresponds to exactly one outcome; a COMPOUND event corresponds to more than one.
Sample SpaceThe full set of all possible outcomes — rolling a die has sample space {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Each element is a sample point.
Mutually ExclusiveThe occurrence of one event excludes the other in that same trial — a coin cannot land both heads AND tails at once. All simple events are mutually exclusive.
Equally LikelyOutcomes with an identical chance of occurring — each face of a fair die is equally likely.
Exhaustive EventsThe COMPLETE set of possible outcomes, with nothing left out. For n coins tossed together, the exhaustive number of outcomes is 2n.
Independent EventsThe occurrence of one does NOT affect the other's probability — two successive coin tosses are independent of each other.
Dependent EventsThe occurrence of one DOES affect the other's probability — drawing a king from a deck WITHOUT replacement changes the probability of drawing a second king.
Complementary EventsTwo mutually exclusive AND exhaustive events, where one is simply “NOT” the other.
Favourable CasesThe specific outcomes that result in the event of interest actually happening.
FORMULA

The Classical (Priori) Approach to Measuring Probability ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Probability of an event = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of mutually exclusive, exhaustive, equally likely outcomes

If an event can occur in ‘a’ ways and fail to occur in ‘b’ ways, p (probability of success) = a/(a+b) and q (probability of failure) = b/(a+b). Since these are the only two possibilities, p+q=1, so 1−p=q and 1−q=p always.

The classical approach has five real limitations.

  1. It applies cleanly only to games of chance, not general real-world problems.
