  2. It cannot be used when the total number of outcomes can't be counted.
  3. It fails when outcomes are NOT equally likely.
  4. Subdividing outcomes into genuinely mutually exclusive, exhaustive, equally likely cases is often difficult in practice.
  5. It somewhat circularly assumes outcomes are equiprobable before actually establishing that they are.

Five classical-probability examples (independently re-verified)

ProblemSolution
Drawing a king from 52 cards4 favourable/52 total = 1/13
Two coins tossed — getting one head and one tail2 favourable (HT,TH)/4 total = 1/2
One card drawn — a diamond? a queen?Diamond: 13/52=1/4. Queen: 4/52=1/13
Two cards drawn — a king and a queen(4×4) / 52C2 = 16/1,326 = 8/663
3 balls from a bag of 7 red, 12 white, 4 green — (i) all white? (ii) one of each colour?(i) 12C3/23C3 = 220/1,771 = 0.1242. (ii) (7C1×12C1×4C1)/1,771 = 336/1,771 = 0.1897
CONCEPT

Relative Frequency (Empirical) Theory of Probability ★★ MEDIUM

The classical approach fails wherever outcomes AREN’T equally likely by nature — a share price moving up, down, or staying flat, for instance, has no natural “equal chance” assumption. The Relative Frequency (or Empirical) approach instead defines probability as the LIMIT of the relative frequency of an event, observed as the number of trials grows very large: P(A) = limn→∞ (m/n), where m is how many times event A occurred across n trials.

This approach has three limitations: experimental conditions may not stay genuinely identical across a large number of repetitions; the relative frequency may never settle on one single, unique value no matter how large N grows; and the true, theoretical P(A) can never actually be observed in practice — only estimated by making N sufficiently large.

FORMULA

Two Further Classical Probability Examples ★★★ HIGH

Drawing two balls from an urn (independently re-verified)

An urn has 8 white and 3 red balls (11 total). Two balls are drawn at random. Find the probability that (a) both are white, (b) both are red, (c) one of each colour.

Exhaustive outcomes = 11C2 = 55.

(a) 8C2/55 = 28/55. (b) 3C2/55 = 3/55. (c) (8C1×3C1)/55 = 24/55.

Numbered tickets, four separate questions (independently re-verified)

Tickets numbered 1 to 100 are shuffled; one is drawn. Find the probability it is (a) even, (b) a multiple of 5, (c) greater than 75, (d) a perfect square.

(a) 50/100 = ½. (b) 20/100 = 1/5 (5,10,…,100 — 20 numbers). (c) 25/100 = ¼ (76–100). (d) 10/100 = 1/10 (1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81,100 — 10 perfect squares).

FORMULA

7.2 The Addition Theorem of Probability ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)

If two events cannot happen together, the probability of EITHER one occurring is simply the sum of their individual probabilities.

A straightforward mutually-exclusive case (independently re-verified)

A bag has 4 white, 3 black, and 5 red balls (12 total). Find the probability of drawing a white OR a red ball.

P(white) + P(red) = 4/12 + 5/12 = 9/12 = 75%.

NOT mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B)

When both events CAN happen together, simply adding their probabilities double-counts the overlap — so that overlap, P(A and B), must be subtracted back out once.

Two students solving a problem independently, verified FOUR different ways (independently re-verified)

P(X solves it)=3/4, P(Y solves it)=2/3, working independently. Find the probability the problem gets solved (i.e. at least one of them solves it).

Method 1, direct formula: P(X or Y) = 3/4+2/3−(3/4×2/3) = 9/12+8/12−6/12 = 11/12.

Method 2, summing 3 disjoint cases (X solves & Y fails; both solve; X fails & Y solves): (3/4×1/3) + (3/4×2/3) + (1/4×2/3) = 3/12+6/12+2/12 = 11/12.

Method 3, via the complement (easiest route): P(neither solves it) = 1/4×1/3 = 1/12, so P(solved) = 1−1/12 = 11/12 — all three methods agree, and the complement method is genuinely the fastest for “at least one” problems.

FORMULA

The Addition Theorem — Three Further Examples ★★★ HIGH

Using exhaustive + equally likely + mutually exclusive together

A, B, C are mutually exclusive, exhaustive, and equally likely. Find P(complement of A).

Since exhaustive: P(A)+P(B)+P(C)=1. Since equally likely: P(A)=P(B)=P(C), so 3×P(A)=1, giving P(A)=1/3.

P(A’) = 1−1/3 = 2/3.

Heart or king (events overlap at the king of hearts)

One card from 52. Find P(heart or king).

P(heart)+P(king)−P(heart and king) = 13/52+4/52−1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.

A coin and a die thrown together

Find P(head or an even number).

P(head)=1/2, P(even)=3/6=1/2. Since the coin and die are independent, P(head and even)=1/2×1/2=1/4.

P(head or even) = 1/2+1/2−1/4 = 3/4.

⚡ SHORTCUT Whenever a question asks for "at least one," it is almost always fastest to compute 1−P(none) rather than adding up every individual/overlapping case directly — illustration 14 above proves this isn't just a shortcut trick, it's mathematically identical to the longer methods.
FORMULA

The Multiplication Theorem of Probability ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Where the Addition Theorem handles “OR,” the Multiplication Theorem handles “AND” — the chance of two or more events happening in SUCCESSION.

Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

Two coin tosses (independently re-verified)

Find the probability of getting heads on BOTH of two tosses.

P(head)×P(head) = 1/2×1/2 = 1/4.

Drawing WITH replacement — a genuine test of independence (independently re-verified)

Two cards are drawn from 52, WITH replacement (the first is put back before the second is drawn). Find P(a) both kings, (b) 1st king & 2nd queen, (c) one king and one queen (either order).

Since the card is replaced, each draw is independent — every draw still has all 52 cards available.

(a) 4/52×4/52 = 1/169. (b) 4/52×4/52 = 1/169. (c) (4/52×4/52)+(4/52×4/52) = 2/169.

Drawing WITHOUT replacement — now the events are dependent (independently re-verified)

Two cards from 52, WITHOUT replacement. Find P(a) both kings, (b) 1st king & 2nd queen.

The first draw removes a card from the pack, so the SECOND draw's probability changes depending on the first outcome — this is exactly what makes without-replacement draws dependent events.

(a) 4/52×3/51 = 1/221. (b) 4/52×4/51 = 4/663.

⚠ TRAP

Replacement changes everything about the second draw

THE TRAP: WITH replacement keeps every draw independent (always 52 cards, always 4 of each rank) — use plain multiplication of unchanged fractions. WITHOUT replacement makes every later draw dependent on earlier ones (fewer cards remain, and the count of a specific rank may have dropped too if it was already drawn) — the denominator (and sometimes numerator) must shrink accordingly at each step.

FORMULA

A Classic Application — Contradictory Statements ★★★ HIGH

Two witnesses, contradicting each other (independently re-verified)

A speaks the truth 70% of the time, B speaks the truth 80% of the time. In what percentage of cases are they likely to CONTRADICT each other?

P(A)=0.7, P(B)=0.8, so P(A’)=0.3, P(B’)=0.2. Contradiction happens when exactly ONE of them is truthful and the other isn’t — two distinct, mutually exclusive ways this can occur.

P(contradiction) = P(A)×P(B’) + P(B)×P(A’) = (0.7×0.2)+(0.8×0.3) = 0.14+0.24 = 0.38, i.e. 38%.

⚡ SHORTCUT "Contradiction" problems always follow this same pattern: (first is right, second is wrong) OR (first is wrong, second is right) — two mutually exclusive terms, ADDED together, each itself a product of two independent probabilities.
FORMULA

Conditional Probability — When Events Are Dependent ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

When A and B are DEPENDENT, B’s probability genuinely changes depending on whether A has already occurred. P(B/A), read “the probability of B given A,” denotes this Conditional Probability.

P(B/A) = P(AB)/P(A)   ·   P(A/B) = P(AB)/P(B)

Rearranged, this gives the general multiplication rule for DEPENDENT events: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B/A) = P(B)·P(A/B) — the with/without-replacement card problems from earlier are really conditional-probability problems in disguise, just solved intuitively rather than via this explicit notation.

Three more independent-events examples, and one "either category" example (independently re-verified)

ProblemSolution
P(X and Y both alive 10 years hence), P(X alive)=0.5, P(Y alive)=0.80.5×0.8 = 0.4
P(a girl with 3 independent qualities, each 1/20, 1/50, 1/100)1/20×1/50×1/100 = 0.00001
P(selecting a Hindi-knowing woman teacher) from 50 candidates: 20 women, 10 Hindi-knowing, 15 teachers20/50×15/50×10/50 = 3/125 = 0.024
From 6 red, 4 white, 5 blue balls (15 total): P(Red), P(white), P(blue), P(not red), P(red or white)6/15=0.4 · 4/15=0.267 · 5/15=0.333 · 9/15=0.6 · 10/15=0.667
CONCEPT

Odds — Chances For vs. Against ★★ MEDIUM

Odds relate the chances IN FAVOUR of an event to the chances AGAINST it. Odds of 2:1 in favour means 2 chances for, 1 chance against.

If the odds are a:b in favour, P(event) = a/(a+b)

Odds of a:b in favour of an event is exactly the same statement as odds of b:a AGAINST it. If probability p is known, the odds in favour are p:(1−p), and the odds against are (1−p):p.

Converting odds, then combining with the Addition Theorem (independently re-verified)

Odds are 11-to-5 AGAINST person A (aged 38) living 35 more years, and 5-to-3 against person B (aged 43) doing the same. Find P(at least one is alive in 35 years).

P(A dies) = 11/16. P(B dies) = 5/8. Since independent, P(both die) = 11/16×5/8 = 55/128.

P(at least one alive) = 1−55/128 = 73/128 ≈ 57%.

Two cards without replacement, three separate questions (independently re-verified)

Two cards drawn from 52, WITHOUT replacement. Find P(a) both aces, (b) both red, (c) at least one ace.

(a) 4/52×3/51 = 1/221. (b) 26/52×25/51 = 25/102. (c) P(no ace either draw) = 48/52×47/51 = 188/221, so P(at least one ace) = 1−188/221 = 33/221.

FORMULA

Bayes' Theorem — Revising Probability With New Information ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Bayes’ Theorem (named for Reverend Thomas Bayes, also called Inverse Probability) revises an existing (“Prior”) probability into an updated (“Posterior”) probability once new information becomes available — genuinely useful whenever a businessperson has EXTRA information beyond the plain base rate, from personal belief or past history.

P(Bi/A) = [P(Bi)·P(A/Bi)] / Σ[P(Bi)·P(A/Bi)]

Where B₁,B₂,…,Bn are mutually exclusive, exhaustive events, and event A can only occur if one of them does. In practice, this is best organised as a table: Prior Probability × Conditional Probability = Joint Probability, then each Joint Probability ÷ the TOTAL of all joint probabilities = the Posterior Probability.

The "happy officer" problem (independently re-verified)

P(officer happy)=0.6, so P(not happy)=0.4. If happy, P(accedes to request)=0.4; if not happy, P(accedes)=0.1. He accedes. Find P(he was happy).

EventPriorConditionalJointPosterior
Happy0.60.40.240.24/0.28 = 6/7
Not happy0.40.10.040.04/0.28 = 1/7
Total1—0.281

P(happy, given he acceded) = 6/7 ≈ 0.857.

FORMULA

Bayes' Theorem — Verified With a Concrete "1,000 Units" Check ★★★ HIGH

Which plant made the standard-quality scooter? (independently re-verified)

Plant I makes 80% of scooters, Plant II makes 20%. Of Plant I’s output, 85% is standard quality; of Plant II’s, 65%. A standard-quality scooter is selected — find P(it came from Plant I) and P(it came from Plant II).

EventPriorConditionalJointPosterior
Plant I0.800.850.680.68/0.81 = 68/81 ≈ 0.840
Plant II0.200.650.130.13/0.81 = 13/81 ≈ 0.160
Total1—0.811

A genuinely helpful sanity check: imagine 1,000 scooters were made. Plant I makes 800, of which 800×85%=680 are standard. Plant II makes 200, of which 200×65%=130 are standard. Of the 680+130=810 standard-quality scooters total, 680 came from Plant I.

P(Plant I | standard) = 680/810 = 68/81 — matching the formula exactly, and making the abstract calculation tangible.

⚡ SHORTCUT When a Bayes' Theorem calculation feels abstract, translate the percentages into a round concrete number (100 or 1,000 units) and count directly — it always matches the formula, and catches setup errors before they compound.

MODULE 7 IN NINETY SECONDS — PROBABILITY, COMPLETE

① Key terms: mutually exclusive (can't both happen) vs independent (one doesn't affect the other's probability) — these are NOT the same thing and get confused constantly.

② Classical approach: P=favourable/total, needs equally-likely outcomes. Relative Frequency: P=lim(m/n) as trials→∞, for cases without natural equal-likelihood.

③ Addition Theorem: P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B) if mutually exclusive; minus P(A and B) if not. "At least one" → often fastest via 1−P(none).

④ Multiplication Theorem: P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B) if independent. WITH replacement stays independent; WITHOUT replacement makes later draws dependent — use P(B/A)=P(AB)/P(A).

⑤ Odds a:b in favour → P=a/(a+b). Odds a:b in favour = odds b:a against.

⑥ Bayes' Theorem revises Prior→Posterior probability using new information: Posterior = Joint/ΣJoint, where Joint=Prior×Conditional. Build the 4-column table every time — verify with a concrete "1,000 units" count if unsure.

MODULE EIGHT OF EIGHT · SECTION B · 10% · THE FINAL MODULE

Index Numbers and Time Series

Two sub-topics closing out the paper: Index Numbers, for measuring how prices, quantities, or values have changed between two periods; and Time Series, for decomposing data collected over time into its underlying trend, seasonal, cyclical, and irregular components.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Laspeyres/Paasche/Fisher/Bowley formulas and how they differ, and the Moving Average method for calculating trend.

8.1–8.2

Module Learning Objectives

Per ICMAI, after studying this Module the students will be able to understand: the concept of Index Numbers and Time Series; the different computation methods and interpretation of results; and the practical application of Index Number and Time Series.

Glossary — Terms Worth Knowing Cold

TermPlain meaning
Index NumberA single ratio (usually %) measuring the combined/averaged change of several variables between two periods.
Base YearThe reference period, always set to an index value of 100.
Current YearThe period being compared against the base year.
Time SeriesData recorded at successive points in time (e.g. monthly sales over 5 years).
CONCEPT

8.1 Index Numbers — Meaning and Types ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

An Index Number is a single ratio, usually expressed as a percentage, measuring the combined (averaged) change of several variables between two periods, places, or situations. If wholesale prices in 2020 index to 250 against a 2010 base, the net increase in wholesale prices was 150%. The BASE year’s value is always set to 100; the CURRENT year is expressed as a percentage of the base.

Simplest Price Index: (Current Price / Base Price) × 100

Index numbers come in five broad types: Price Index (change in prices), Quantity Index (change in quantities produced/consumed), Value Index (change in total value, i.e. price×quantity), Diffusion Index, and others.

Construction methods split into two families — Aggregative (or Average) methods and Average of Relatives methods — and each further splits into Simple and Weighted versions. Within Weighted Aggregative specifically, four NAMED methods matter most: Laspeyres’, Paasche’s, Fisher’s, and Bowley’s.

FORMULA

Simple and Weighted Aggregative Methods ★★★ HIGH

Simple Aggregative: P01 = (ΣP₁/ΣP₀) × 100

Simple aggregative price index (independently re-verified)

Five commodities’ prices sum to ₹42.30 in the base year and ₹52.95 in the current year.

P01 = 52.95/42.30 × 100 = 125.18 — prices rose about 25% overall.

Simple aggregative has two real limitations: it is distorted by whatever UNITS the commodities happen to be quoted in, giving some commodities outsized influence purely from unit choice; and high-priced commodities dominate the index regardless of their actual importance in typical consumption.

Weighted Aggregative: P01 = (ΣP₁W/ΣP₀W) × 100

W is a weight (usually quantity) attached to each commodity, fixing the unit/importance distortion above.

Weighted aggregative price index (independently re-verified)

Three commodities with quantities (weights) 7, 8, 4. Working out P×W for both base and current prices gives ΣP₀W=3.575, ΣP₁W=5.823.

P01 = 5.823/3.575 × 100 = 162.88.

FORMULA

The Four Named Methods — One Dataset, All Four Answers ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

MethodFormula
Laspeyres'P01 = (ΣP₁Q₀/ΣP₀Q₀)×100 — uses BASE year quantities as weights
Paasche'sP01 = (ΣP₁Q₁/ΣP₀Q₁)×100 — uses CURRENT year quantities as weights
Fisher'sP01 = √(Laspeyres×Paasche) — the “ideal” index, geometric mean of the other two
Bowley'sP01 = (Laspeyres+Paasche)/2 — simple arithmetic mean of the other two

All four methods applied to the same 4-commodity dataset (independently re-verified)

CommodityP₁P₀Q₁Q₀P₁Q₀P₀Q₀P₁Q₁P₀Q₁
A2.52121025203024
B3.21.8101651.228.83218
C4.83.58838.42838.428
D42.810124833.64028
Total162.6110.4140.498

Laspeyres = 162.6/110.4×100 = 147.28. Paasche = 140.4/98×100 = 143.27. Fisher = √(1.4728×1.4327)×100 = 145.26. Bowley = (1.4728+1.4327)/2×100 = 145.27.

⚡ SHORTCUT Remember which quantity anchors which method: LaspeyRes uses base-yeaR quantities (Q₀); PaaSche uses current-year quantitieS (Q₁). Fisher and Bowley both just COMBINE Laspeyres and Paasche — Fisher via geometric mean (√), Bowley via simple average.
CONCEPT

Laspeyres vs. Paasche — Why They Differ, and Why Fisher Is "Ideal" ★★★ HIGH

Though both are Weighted Aggregative methods, Laspeyres’ and Paasche’s differ in a genuinely important way.

  1. Laspeyres’ uses BASE year quantities as weights, so it does NOT capture how quantity demanded shifted in response to price changes. Paasche’s, using CURRENT year quantities, DOES capture this shift.
  2. Laspeyres’ represents the cost of maintaining the SAME base-year consumption pattern at current prices. Paasche’s represents the actual cost of current consumption compared to the base year.
  3. Laspeyres’ is typically UPWARD biased; Paasche’s is typically DOWNWARD biased.

Fisher's method is called the Ideal Index for three reasons.

  1. It is largely free from bias, since Laspeyres' upward pull and Paasche's downward pull tend to cancel out.
  2. It accounts for BOTH the base and current year's quantities together.
  3. It rests on the geometric mean, theoretically the best average for constructing index numbers.
FORMULA

The Relatives Method ★★ MEDIUM

Price Relative = (Current year price / Base year price) × 100

Each commodity’s current price is expressed as a percentage of its OWN base price first, before any averaging happens.

MethodFormula
Simple Average of Relatives (AM)P01 = (1/n)Σ(P₁/P₀×100)
Simple Average of Relatives (GM)P01 = Antilog[Σlog(P₁/P₀×100)/n]
Weighted Average of RelativesP01 = Σ[(P₁/P₀×100)×w] / Σw

The Relatives method takes each commodity’s OWN percentage change first, so unlike the Aggregative methods, it is naturally unaffected by whatever units the commodities happen to be quoted in.

FORMULA

Quantity Index — the Same Formulas, Applied to Quantities ★★ MEDIUM

Every method built for the Price Index has a direct parallel for the Quantity Index — simply swap the roles of P and Q throughout each formula.

MethodFormula
Simple AggregativeQ01 = (ΣQ₁/ΣQ₀)×100
Laspeyres'Q01 = (ΣQ₁P₀/ΣQ₀P₀)×100 — uses BASE year PRICES as weights
Paasche'sQ01 = (ΣQ₁P₁/ΣQ₀P₁)×100 — uses CURRENT year PRICES as weights
⚡ SHORTCUT Price Index asks "how much did PRICE change, holding a fixed basket of quantities?" Quantity Index asks the mirror question: "how much did QUANTITY change, holding a fixed set of prices?" Every formula pair mirrors this — just swap which variable is fixed (the weight) and which one varies.
FORMULA

General Index From Group Indices ★★ MEDIUM

When commodities are divided into related GROUPS, each group gets its own Group Index first. The overall General Index is then the weighted arithmetic mean of those group indices.

General Index = ΣwI / Σw

I = each Group Index, w = that group’s weight.

FORMULA

Deriving Price Relatives From Percentage Statements ★★★ HIGH

A distinctive, frequently-tested problem type gives ONLY percentage relationships between years’ prices — never raw prices. The technique: ASSUME the most convenient year equals 100, derive the others algebraically, then re-express everything relative to whichever year is actually asked for as the base.

Two years' relationships to a third (independently re-verified)

In 2023, price was 20% MORE than in 2022, but 20% LESS than in 2021. Find price relatives using 2022 as base.

Assume 2023=100. Since 2023 is 20% more than 2022: 2022 = 100/1.20 = 83.33. Since 2023 is 20% less than 2021: 2021 = 100/0.80 = 125.

Re-basing to 2022 (83.33): 2021 = 150, 2022 = 100, 2023 = 120.

Using an AVERAGE of two years as the base (independently re-verified)

In 2022, price was 20% more than 2021, but 50% more than 2023. Find price relatives using the average of 2021 & 2022 as base.

Assume 2022=100. Then 2021 = 100/1.20 = 83.33, and 2023 = 100/1.50 = 66.67. Average of 2021 & 2022 = (83.33+100)/2 = 91.67.

Re-basing to 91.67: 2021 ≈ 90.9, 2022 ≈ 109.1, 2023 ≈ 72.7.

⚡ SHORTCUT "X% more than Y" means Y×(1+X/100)=the given value — so working BACKWARD, Y = given value/(1+X/100). "X% less than Y" works the same way with (1−X/100) instead. Always assume the year mentioned FIRST or most directly in the problem equals 100 to simplify the algebra.
CONCEPT

8.2 Time Series — Components and Models ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

A Time Series is data recorded over successive points in time — daily, monthly, quarterly, or yearly. Analysing a time series means analysing history, used by management for long-term forecasting and current decisions.

A time series has four components.

  1. Trend (T): the smoothed, long-term direction of the series — also called the Secular Trend.
  2. Cyclical Fluctuation (C): longer, wave-like swings, often tied to business cycles.
  3. Seasonal Variation (S): regular, predictable fluctuations tied to the calendar (quarters, months, seasons).
  4. Irregular Movement (I): random, unpredictable fluctuation left over after the other three are accounted for.
BasisAdditive ModelMultiplicative Model
FormulaY = T+C+S+IY = T×C×S×I
S, C, I areAbsolute quantitative deviationsRates, percentages, or index numbers
ComponentsAssumed independent of each otherCan affect one another
ForecastingNot well-suited to future extensionRelative values ARE suited to forecasting
Real-world useRare in practiceMost economic/business data fit this — the model this Module focuses on
FORMULA

Moving Average — Smoothing Out the Fluctuations ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

A Moving Average smooths a time series to reveal its Trend, by sliding an arithmetic mean of ‘n’ consecutive values through the whole series. Choosing n depends on the data’s natural cycle — 4 for quarterly data, 7 for daily (a week), or found via trial and error otherwise. Each computed average is positioned against the MIDDLE year of its own group.

Complete 7-year moving average, 26 years of sales data (independently re-verified)

Sales (₹ million), 1988–2013. The first 7-year total (1988–1994): 1+2+3+4+5+4+3=22, average=22/7=3.143, positioned at the group's middle year, 1991. The next group shifts forward by one year (1989–1995), and so on through the last group (2007–2013).

YearSales7yr Total7yr AvgYearSales7yr Total7yr Avg
19881——20014324.571
19892——20023334.714
19903——20034344.857
19914223.14320045355.000
19925233.28620056365.143
19934243.42920067375.286
19943253.57120076385.429
19952263.71420085395.571
19963273.85720094405.714
19974284.00020105415.857
19985294.14320116——
19996304.28620127——
20005314.42920138——

The first and last 3 years of any 7-year moving average always stay blank — there aren’t enough neighbouring years to centre a group on them.

FORMULA

Even-Numbered Moving Averages — the Centering Step ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

With an ODD n (like 7), each group has one natural middle year. With an EVEN n (like 4 or 6), a group has no single middle year — its moving total sits BETWEEN two years instead. Fixing this needs one extra step: Centering, averaging each pair of adjacent moving averages so the result lines up with an actual year again.

4-year moving average with centering (independently re-verified)

Sales, 2005–2013: 8, 11, 9, 14, 9, 10, 10, 8, 12. The 1st 4-year total (2005–2008) = 8+11+9+14 = 42, average = 10.5 — but this has no single middle year, so it’s positioned BETWEEN 2006 and 2007.

Successive 4-year moving averages: 10.5, 10.75, 10.5, 10.75, 9.25, 10.0 (each still between two years). Centering pairs adjacent averages together: (10.5+10.75)/2=10.625 for 2007; (10.75+10.5)/2=10.625 for 2008; (10.5+10.75)/2=10.625 for 2009; (10.75+9.25)/2=10.0 for 2010; (9.25+10.0)/2=9.625 for 2011.

The final 4-year Centred Moving Average column: 2007→10.625, 2008→10.625, 2009→10.625, 2010→10.0, 2011→9.625.

⚡ SHORTCUT Odd n → one middle year per group, done in a single averaging pass. Even n → the moving average sits BETWEEN years, so a second centering pass (averaging adjacent pairs) is always required to land back on real years. Never skip centering for even-n data — an un-centred even moving average is genuinely mispositioned, not just imprecise.

MODULE 8 IN NINETY SECONDS — INDEX NUMBERS & TIME SERIES, COMPLETE

① Index Number: (Current/Base)×100. Simple Aggregative=ΣP₁/ΣP₀×100. Weighted Aggregative=ΣP₁W/ΣP₀W×100.

② Laspeyres uses BASE-year quantities (upward bias). Paasche uses CURRENT-year quantities (downward bias). Fisher=√(L×P), the "ideal" index. Bowley=(L+P)/2.

③ Quantity Index mirrors Price Index with P/Q swapped. Price Relative=(P₁/P₀)×100 — unaffected by units, unlike Aggregative methods.

④ Time Series has 4 components: Trend, Cyclical, Seasonal, Irregular. Multiplicative model (Y=T×C×S×I) fits most real economic data; Additive (Y=T+C+S+I) is rare in practice.

⑤ Moving Average smooths fluctuations to reveal Trend. Odd n → one middle year per group. Even n → the average falls between years, needing a CENTERING pass (average adjacent pairs) to land back on real years.

The Master Trap List — 30 Distractors This Paper Is Built From

Every MCQ distractor and every half-remembered numerical in this paper traces back to one of these confusions. Read once, slowly, the morning of the exam.

1. “Duplicate ratio” means SQUARED, not doubled — a:b compounded with itself gives a²:b², not 2a:2b (which is just the same ratio again, by the scaling property).

2. Direct and inverse variation isolate K differently — direct: K=A/B (a ratio); inverse: K=A×B (a product). Confusing which operation isolates K is the single most common slip.

3. An annuity needs BOTH a constant interval AND a constant amount — a sequence of deposits with either alone, but not both, is a “multiple flow,” not an annuity.

4. When an unknown is found from a SMALL difference between two compounding results (like C.I.−S.I.), 2-decimal table rounding can swing the answer by several percent — carry extra decimal places.

5. Annuity due = regular annuity × (1+r), always — for both Future Value and Present Value, since each flow lands one extra period earlier and compounds one period more.

6. De Morgan's Law flips the operation, not just the sets — complementing a UNION gives an INTERSECTION, and complementing an INTERSECTION gives a UNION.

7. “nCr=1” is not a general property — it only holds for r=0 or r=n. The identity worth memorising is nCn=1, paired with nC0=1.

8. Always recompute a power by hand rather than trust a printed answer — (2.5)⁵ correctly shown as five factors of 2.5 multiplied together equals 97.65625, not the 244.14062 that six factors would give.

9. For the same n and r, Permutation is always LARGER than Combination, by a factor of r! — because permutation additionally counts every different ORDER of the same selected group.

10. Pascal's Law, nCr−1+nCr=n+1Cr, is a provable identity, not a coincidence — it is the exact relationship that builds Pascal's Triangle.

11. A quadratic “in disguise” (fractional powers, an infinite nested radical, an infinite continued fraction) collapses by naming the WHOLE expression x, substituting x back into itself one level in, and simplifying.

12. Marginal Cost is INDEPENDENT of Fixed Cost — since fixed cost never changes with output, there is no such thing as “marginal fixed cost.”

13. A cubic Profit function's first-order condition is quadratic — expect TWO critical points, and only the second-derivative test (negative=max, positive=min) tells them apart; never assume the larger or smaller root is automatically the answer.

14. Unequal class widths need Frequency Density, not raw frequency, as the histogram's bar height — otherwise wide classes look misleadingly “taller” just because they span more ground.

15. Inclusive series (0–5, 6–10) INCLUDES the upper limit in its own class; Exclusive series (10–15, 15–20) pushes the shared boundary value into the NEXT class instead.

16. Coefficient of Variation and Skewness can genuinely diverge on the same pair of distributions — two series can share identical skewness while differing in variability, or vice versa; always check BOTH independently, never assume one implies the other.

17. Swapping which value is Mean and which is Mode flips the SIGN of Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness entirely — check the sign before the magnitude.

18. Standard Deviation is independent of change of ORIGIN but NOT of change of SCALE — shifting every value by a constant leaves S.D. unchanged; multiplying every value by a constant scales S.D. by that same constant.

19. Correlation never proves causation — it only measures co-variation; two variables can move together from a common cause, mutual dependence, or pure chance, and r alone cannot distinguish between these.

20. Regression is NOT symmetric like correlation — there are always TWO distinct lines (Y on X, and X on Y), and mixing up byx with bxy is the single most common error in this topic.

21. A fairly large r can still fail the significance test — r must exceed 6×Probable Error to count as significant; r=0.69 with P.E.=0.118 (6×P.E.=0.708) is NOT significant despite looking substantial.

22. “High negative correlation” is the range −1<r<−0.75, mirroring the positive side's structure exactly — not any range that puts 1 on the wrong side of −0.75.

23. Mutually Exclusive and Independent are NOT the same thing — mutually exclusive means the events cannot both happen in one trial; independent means one occurring does not change the other's probability.

24. Drawing WITH replacement keeps every draw independent; WITHOUT replacement makes later draws dependent — the denominator (and sometimes the numerator) must shrink at each subsequent step.

25. For “at least one” problems, compute 1−P(none) — almost always the fastest route, and mathematically identical to summing every individual and overlapping case.

26. Odds a:b IN FAVOUR of an event equal odds b:a AGAINST it — reversing the ratio without reversing which side it favours is a common slip.

27. Laspeyres' uses BASE-year quantities as weights (typically upward biased); Paasche's uses CURRENT-year quantities (typically downward biased) — swapping which year's quantities belong to which method is the most common error in this topic.

28. An even-n Moving Average (4-year, 6-year, etc.) has no single middle year and must be CENTRED — averaging adjacent pairs — before it lines up with a real year again; skipping this step leaves the trend genuinely mispositioned, not just imprecise.

29. “X% more than Y” means Y×(1+X/100) = the given value, so working backward, Y = given value ÷ (1+X/100) — not the “X% less than” formula, which instead divides by (1−X/100).

30. The two ogive curves cross at exactly one point, and reading straight down from that crossing to the x-axis gives the Median — a graphical shortcut that skips the formula-based calculation entirely.

The Last 48 Hours — Revision Plan for This Document
WhenWhat to do
48 hours outRe-read Modules 2 and 1 end to end — Algebra (20%, the single largest module: sets, indices/logarithms, permutation & combination, quadratic equations) and Arithmetic (15%: ratios/variations/proportions, time value of money, AP/GP, time & distance). Together these are 35% of the paper. Re-attempt every worked example cold, covering the solution first.
36 hours outRe-read Modules 5, 6, and 7 — Central Tendency & Dispersion, Correlation & Regression, and Probability, each 15% and together the statistical core of the paper (45% combined). Rehearse the formula-heavy comparison tables out loud: Karl Pearson's vs Bowley's skewness, byx vs bxy, the Addition vs Multiplication theorem.
24 hours outSweep Module 8 (Index Numbers & Time Series, 10%) and Module 3 (Calculus, 5%) — lighter modules, but full marks if their formula tables are drilled cold: Laspeyres/Paasche/Fisher/Bowley, and MR=MC with the first/second-derivative test.
18 hours outSweep Module 4 (Statistical Representation of Data, 5%) — the lightest module in the paper and the cheapest marks per minute: the pie-chart angle formula, class boundary/class mark, frequency density for unequal widths, and the ogive-crossing-equals-median shortcut.
6 hours outRead The Final Ladder above, start to finish, once, slowly.
2 hours outRead the Master Trap List above, start to finish, once, slowly. Nothing new after this point.
In the hallNo negative marking — attempt every question. Skim the full paper first, then work the modules you feel surest of before the heavier Algebra and Statistics numericals. Open every numerical by naming the formula or theorem it needs before starting the calculation — it catches a wrong setup before it wastes minutes.

Weight-based priority if time runs out anywhere in this plan: Module 2 (20%, Algebra) is never the one you cut — it alone outweighs Modules 3 and 4 combined. Modules 1, 5, 6, and 7 (15% each, 60% combined) come next, roughly interchangeable in urgency. Module 8 (10%) and Module 4 (5%) reward memorising a handful of formulas over broad reading — a focused pass on just the Laspeyres/Paasche/Fisher/Bowley table, or the pie-chart angle formula, recovers most of their marks fast. Module 3 (5%, Calculus) is the smallest module in the paper and the fastest to shore up, since it is only three formula families: differentiation rules, MR=MC, and the first/second-derivative test.

This page is exam strategy, not syllabus content — every fact it points to lives in the verified module pages above, condensed strictly from ICMAI's own Paper 3 Study Notes.
